modules.name: Anatomy & Physiology of Speech, Language & Hearing
modules.desc: The four subsystems of speech (respiration, phonation, resonation, articulation), the brain's speech/language centers and neural pathways, and the anatomy of the hearing mechanism.

modules.name: Language Acquisition: Theories & Communication Foundations
modules.desc: Communication foundations (terminology, framework, Hockett's design features, the speech chain, brain), the nature–nurture debate, and the three theory families — nativism, behaviorism, and interactionism — with Chomsky's LAD and transformational grammar, Skinner's operant conditioning, and the interactionist views (Vygotsky, Piaget, semantic/cognitive/social).

modules.name: Theories of Language Development
modules.desc: A deeper look at the major theories of language acquisition and their theorists: nativism (Chomsky/LAD), behaviorism (Skinner's operant conditioning, verbal operants, and Pavlov's classical conditioning), and the interactionist views — semantic (Fillmore), cognitive (Piaget), social interactionist (Bruner/LASS), and the pragmatics revolution (Austin & Searle) — plus evidence and limitations (virtuous errors, the critical period/Genie, creoles).

modules.name: Cognitive Development
modules.desc: Piaget's cognitive development: how knowledge is organized (schema, assimilation, accommodation, equilibrium) and his four stages (sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operations, formal operations), with a detailed look at the six key sensorimotor skills and six substages that lay the groundwork for language.

modules.name: Communication Development: Birth to 2 Years
modules.desc: How communication develops from birth to age 2: influencing factors and SES/the word gap, parent-child and child-directed interactions (contingent responding, joint reference, parentese, expansion/extension), word learning (fast vs. slow mapping, phonological representations, three meaning hypotheses), prelinguistic vocal development (Bates' stages; cooing through jargon), gestures and pointing, and first words (over/underextension, Halliday, Dore, MLU).

modules.name: Cognitive Development II: Vygotsky
modules.desc: Vygotsky's sociocultural theory of cognitive development: private speech, the zone of proximal development and scaffolding, shape bias, the development of perception (visual-tactile and auditory), executive functions, controlled attention and working memory (phonological loop and visual-spatial sketchpad), and theory of mind.

modules.name: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples
modules.desc: Early syntactic development and language-sample analysis: morphemes (free/bound, derivational/inflectional), Brown's stages and 14 grammatical morphemes with the 90% obligatory-context criterion, two-word semantic relations, the mathetic/informative/pragmatic functions, comprehension before production, and how to collect a language sample and calculate mean length of utterance (MLU).

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The body region located below the diaphragm.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: Intrinsic laryngeal muscles that move the vocal folds apart (away from midline), opening the glottis.
Variations in pronunciation of sounds, modulation of pitch or tone, and prominence of syllables or words during speech.
Cognitive process whereby new schemes are created for information that does not fit existing schemes.
Spontaneous description of an event or experience without prompting from an adult.
Changes children make to their schemes in order to fit into and function within their environment when experiencing cognitive conflict, achieved through assimilation or accommodation.

Strategy whereby teachers add to an existing curriculum to take cultures other than the dominant culture into account by expanding content and introducing culturally related concepts, themes, and perspectives without altering the basic structure of the curriculum.
Environment in which children are encouraged to retain their first language and to embrace their native culture while learning the majority language and also embracing a second culture.
Connects two or more sentences, clauses, or parts of clauses by adding more information to what is already there (and, in addition, also); the first conjunctive relation developed by children.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: Intrinsic laryngeal muscles that bring the vocal folds together (toward midline), closing the glottis for phonation.
Word or phrase that modifies a noun and can be an adjective (pretty, tall), an ordinal (second, last), or a quantifier (one, couple, few).

Word that describes or changes the meaning of a verb or verb phrase, but it also qualifies adjectives, other adverbs, and clauses. Adverbs often end in -ly and answer wh-questions, such as how, when, where, and why.

Adverb that connects two clauses and demonstrates addition (furthermore, equally important), a time sequence (simultaneously, after a while), contrast (in spite of, regardless), comparison (likewise, also), or other relationships.

Clause that expresses information about the speaker's attitude towards the content of the sentence, possibly intended to focus attention on the speaker's purpose, apart from or in addition to the communication ("To be quite honest with you, you're making a mistake").
Coordinating conjunctions used to express comparisons or contrasts with regard to the main clause of the sentence (e.g., but, yet, still, however, although).

As new learning occurs, this phenomenon allows the neural network to retain its plasticity and its stability in word representations so that word learning increases efficiently across time. This effect is associated with the tendency for words that are learned earlier to show faster retrieval during naming and reading tasks than words learned later.
Words that refer to things that cause action.
Grammatical form that denotes the doer of a given action, often (but not always) accomplished by adding an -er to a verb in order to change it into a noun (e.g., a person who teaches is a teacher).
One speech sound among a set of sounds used to pronounce a single phoneme.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The hard, bumpy ridge directly behind the top front teeth; an articulation landmark.
Reading level that activates a reader's deep processing of the information.
Type of reference in which a pronoun is used to refer to something in a preceding utterance.
Nouns that refer to living things.
Feature or characteristic of a speech sound is anticipated during the production of a preceding speech sound.

Idea that there is nothing inherent in a spoken word to account for its meaning, no limitation to what language can describe, and no explicit or necessary connection between sounds used and the message being sent; Charles Hockett's eighth "design-feature" of language.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The nerve-fiber bundle that transmits language information, connecting Wernicke's area to Broca's area.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The fourth subsystem of speech: refining sound by restricting or interrupting the airstream with the articulators. Most associated with shaping consonant sounds.
A disorder in the use of the speech mechanism to form the necessary place, manner, and voicing of sounds.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The movable and fixed structures that shape speech sounds: teeth, tongue, lips, alveolar ridge, hard palate, soft palate (velum), and jaw.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: Pyramid-shaped cartilages that sit atop the cricoid. Each has a vocal process and a lateral process; muscles move the lateral processes to bring the vocal folds together or apart.
Release of air on the production of phonemes during speech.
Cognitive process whereby a new stimulus is fitted into an existing schema.
Form of simplification during speech in which one sound takes on the identity (or some of the characteristics) of another sound.
Process by which a dominant first language fades, and a second language becomes dominant.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The nerve that connects to the cochlea and carries hearing messages to the brain.
Group of developmental disabilities, with an onset before 36 months of age, that can cause significant social, communication, and behavioral challenges.
One of Skinner's verbal operants: putting words together based on one's observations and experiences.
"Helping" verb, such as be, do, or have, that accompanies a main verb and expresses tense, aspect, modality, voice, or emphasis.
Warning that there will be an unpleasant consequence for a particular behavior.
The behaviorist who argued language is learned through operant conditioning (reinforcement and punishment).
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Combinations of vowel- and consonant-like sounds produced without meaning.
The theory that language is a learned behavior shaped mainly by the environment (an argument for NURTURE).
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Process of acquiring two languages from birth and becoming competent in both languages at a relatively equal rate.
Process of acquiring one language before exposure to a second language.
Theorists who argue oral language is instinctive and genetically coded, produced with minimal environmental input.
glossary.source: Born to Talk, Ch. 2: Language Acquisition — A Theoretical Journey

glossary.def: Reading activity in which caregivers engage in interactive reading with a child.
Morphemes that are attached to words and cannot stand alone (e.g., possessive form of -s).

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: If a gas is kept at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional (and have a constant product). Explains inhalation/exhalation: as thoracic volume increases, pressure drops and air rushes in; as volume decreases, pressure rises and air flows out.
Idea that the sound of speech is heard in all directions but listeners interpret it as coming from one specific direction; Charles Hockett's second "design-feature" of language.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A left-hemisphere region responsible for the motor planning and coordination of articulation.
A framework that links mean length of utterance (MLU) ranges to stages (I-V) and approximate ages, tracking the progression of grammar and syntax.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

glossary.def: A specific semantic role or function that a particular type of noun phrase can fill; the verb determines which cases its nouns take (e.g., agentive, dative, instrumental, locative).

Semantic theory developed by Charles Fillmore to explain the importance and influence of semantics on the form of language; a form of generative grammar that describes the deep structure of sentences in terms of the relation of a verb to a set of semantic cases.
One clause expresses an action or state of being, and the other clause provides a reason or describes the effect.
Understanding that people, objects, or events can have an effect on other people, objects, or events.

Organizational narrative structure that involves building a story around a central theme with each item or action in the narrative being connected to the central theme by an attribute that is related to the theme.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The brain and spinal cord; the pathway along which speech and language messages travel from the brain toward the muscles of speech.
Stroke; damage to the brain due to a lack of blood flow and oxygen.

Instructional procedure that involves reinforcing individual responses occurring in a sequence to form a complex behavior; organizational narrative structure that involves ordering events so that one event logically follows the preceding event.
The specially adapted way caregivers talk to children to support language acquisition (also called motherese/parentese).
Process of placing words into categories based on their semantic relationships.
Variation of conditioned learning in which an originally neutral stimulus is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus that elicits a desired response.

A disorder that involves both speech and language errors including sound omissions and distortions, irregular rate and lack of pausing, poor awareness and self-monitoring, incomplete phrases, and disorganization in the construction and execution of verbal information.
During rapid speech, a speech sound is influenced by, and becomes more like, a preceding or following speech sound.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The spiral, snail-shell-shaped structure of the inner ear (within the temporal bone) responsible for hearing.
Combinations of words or phrases from more than one language.
An interactionist view holding that language is neither purely innate nor purely learned, but reflects and parallels cognitive development.
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: A researcher who studied pre-verbal parent-infant interaction and concluded that the turn-taking structure of conversation develops through games and non-verbal exchange before words appear.
Sending and receiving information, ideas, feelings, or messages.
A model that divides communication into SPEECH (articulation, phonology, fluency, voice) and LANGUAGE (semantics, morphology, syntax, pragmatics); components of one can influence the other.
glossary.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Situation in which a communicative event takes place.
Adjective used to compare one noun to another noun; occurs through the addition of the suffix -er.
Reading level that requires a reader to use all the other reading levels to reflect on information from multiple sources in order to compare meanings.
A speaker's underlying knowledge of the rules of their language; nativists stress competence over performance.
glossary.source: Born to Talk, Ch. 2: Language Acquisition — A Theoretical Journey

glossary.def: Piaget's third stage (7 to 11 years); logical thinking and growth in reading/writing, but still limited in abstract thinking.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

glossary.def: The learned reaction to a conditioned stimulus.
A previously neutral stimulus that, after association, comes to trigger a learned response.

Hearing loss that occurs due to poor transmission of information from the outer or middle ear to the inner ear, with the most common causes being fluid in the middle ear, malformations of the outer ear, impacted cerumen, perforation or inflammation of the tympanic membrane, or poor functioning of the tiny bones of the middle ear (malleus, incus, and stapes).
Process of combining and joining language constructions.
Second phase of writing development in which a child writes strings of words using the same vocabulary and rules of grammar used in his own speech.
Group of two or more consonant sounds that come before, after, or between vowels.
Parent's prompt response to a child's behavior or verbalization.
Reduction or shortening of a pronoun and verb phrase (e.g., he's running).

Strategy whereby teachers include information on selected heroes and holidays from a range of cultures, and they focus on a few specific characteristics of these cultures while maintaining the existing curriculum.
Capacity to maintain and hold relevant information, especially when there are internal or external distractions or interferences in the environment.
Revision, clarification, or repetition of a message to increase the chances of successful communication.
Forms of interactive communication between two or more people.
Production of vowel-like sounds and brief consonant-like sound during the first few months.
Word used to link the subject and predicate of a sentence; main verb.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The 12 pairs of nerves that transmit sensory and motor information; 6 are primarily associated with motor speech.
Language that develops as a result of contact between two groups that do not know each other's language.

Hypotheses which suggests that African American Vernacular English is a complicated hybrid derived from several African languages and Portuguese, Dutch, French, and English as a result of the early contact between Africans and Europeans.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A ring-shaped cartilage that sits within the thyroid cartilage at its base.
A developmental window (roughly up to about age 7) after which a first language is unlikely to be fully acquired.
Research about language or language development that looks for universal patterns among various languages.
Knowledge students must learn regarding the world that is shared at particular grade levels, regardless of cultural backgrounds of individual students.
Five places along the eastern and southern coasts of the United States from which most regional dialects have evolved: Boston, Philadelphia, tidewater Virginia, Charleston, and New Orleans.
Average age of a group of children at which a particular phoneme is produced with more than 50% accuracy in at least two word positions.
A theorist who modified Chomsky's LAD, proposing it is less a set of fixed linguistic categories and more a process mechanism the child uses to work out the rules of language.
Devoid of situation or context.
Process by which a creole language becomes increasingly similar to the language of the dominant culture.
In Chomsky's transformational grammar, the underlying syntactic structure of a sentence generated by phrase-structure rules.
Imitating a behavior later by retrieving it from memory (without the model present); emerges in sensorimotor substage 6 and supports communication and play.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

glossary.def: Use of pointing, showing, or reaching for something to call attention to or indicate an object or event.

Words bound to either a linguistic or extralinguistic context for their interpretation that specify identity, spatial, or temporal location from the perspective of a speaker or listener in the context in which the message occurs (here/there, this/that, and I/you).

Phenomenon in which understanding the meaning of certain words and phrases in an utterance requires contextual information; message interpretation depends on extralinguistic contexts, such as who is speaking, time, place, location, and gestures of the speaker.
More complex form of imitation whereby an action or behavior is repeated some time after the model.
Signal indicating that reinforcement will not follow a particular response.
Morphemes added to the beginning (e.g., re-, un-) and end (e.g., -ly, -un) of words; prefixes and suffixes.
First unit in a noun phrase that is an article (a, the), a possessive pronoun (my, his, her), a demonstrative pronoun (this, that, these, those), or a qualifier (some, most, any).

Individuals who are not yet reading independently, but read for meaning using the text, illustrations, letter-sound associations, and their own knowledge of print conventions to sample, predict, and confirm printed words.
Broad term used when a disability occurs prior to the age of 22 and is associated with mental or physical impairments.
Any given variety of a language shared by a group of speakers.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The primary muscle of inhalation, a dome-shaped muscle sitting just below the lungs. When it contracts it flattens, enlarging the thorax; at rest it returns to its dome shape, driving exhalation.

Third stage of writing development in which students' writing becomes differentiated from the way they talk through the use of more sophisticated grammar; this stage continues for many people throughout their lives.
Listener can compare the loudness and timing of sound reaching each ear and can determine the direction from where the sound is coming; Charles Hockett's second "design-feature" of language.
When an object has been present, but then disappears; words used to express this relationship may be bye-bye.

Idea that each language is limited to a finite or discrete number of sounds. Furthermore, each sound used in one or more human languages has very specific characteristics and can be placed in distinct categories that differentiate them from one another; Charles Hockett's ninth "design-feature" of language.
Stimulus, such as a cue, that provides information about what to do.
Human ability to refer to things in space and time and communicate about things that are not currently present; Charles Hockett's 10th "design-feature" of language.
Ability to use an abstract symbol or word to represent the real object. Language is the way humans represent people, places, and things in thought and interactions.
View that speech sounds comprise characteristics of place of articulation, manner of articulation, and voicing.

Concept that a child who is exposed to two languages from birth uses two separate language systems from the very beginning and does not go through stages in which a conjoined language system is gradually differentiated into two language systems.

The restricted number of sounds in a given language can be combined in an infinite number of ways to produce an infinite variety of words, which in turn are combined again to make meaningful sentences; Charles Hockett's 12th "design-feature" of language.

Second stage of spelling development in which a child often only attends to the first letter of a word, uses consonants but excludes vowels, and other letters typically have no correspondence to the remaining segments of the target word.
The lower range of Brown's Stage I (MLU ~1.0-1.5): mostly single words with some early two-word combinations.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

glossary.def: One of Skinner's verbal operants: imitation of a model when objects or ideas are present.
Imitation or repetition of words, phrases, or whole sentences spoken by another person.
Placing new strings of words within already existing constructions.
Individuals who are not yet reading, but are just beginning to grasp the basic concepts of books and print and developing alphabetical knowledge and phonological awareness skills.
The behaviorist metaphor of the child's mind as a blank container that the environment fills with language.
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck
Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A cartilage attached to the cricoid. It contributes little to speech but plays a major role in protecting the windpipe during swallowing.
Cognitive process to maintain a balance between existing schemata (assimilation) and the creation of new schemata (accommodation).
Order or sequence of events taking place in a story.

A set of control processes in the brain that let us maintain attention, inhibit irrelevant associations, and use working memory; not fully developed until the mid-20s (which helps explain impulsive decisions in children, teens, and young adults).
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

glossary.def: When an object is present in a child's immediate environment and the child is attending to it; words used to express this relationship may be this, that, and there.
When an adult repeats what a child has said adding additional words and/or structure to the utterance.
Use of components including introductory information, background information, and evaluations (emphasis and meaning) to generate more creative and meaningful narratives.
Producing and conveying communicative messages through speaking, writing, signing, or gestures.
When an adult repeats a child's utterance adding additional words, structure, and new information to the utterance.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The ear canal, running from the pinna to the eardrum.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A special pathway of the central nervous system controlling more gross and unskilled motor movements.
Act of learning a new concept after limited exposure, commonly used by young children when acquiring language.
Nonliteral form of language used to describe something by comparing it with something else (e.g., idioms, similes, metaphors, and irony).
Objects that have value, but do not do anything (e.g., money); wealth of the individual within a society.
A child's initial words that convey meaning in a purposeful, consistent, and specific way.
The smoothness, rate, and continuity (flow) of connected speech.
glossary.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Piaget's fourth stage (11 to 15 years); the ability to think abstractly, use prior knowledge with new information, and plan for tasks.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)
Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: Respiration, Phonation, Resonation, and Articulation — the ordered chain of subsystems that produce speech. All the structures involved are designed for other, more basic biological purposes.
A morpheme that can stand alone as a complete word (e.g., 'dog', 'run').
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

glossary.def: Vowel and consonant sounds with a full range of frequencies and resonant characteristics.

Idea that children do not categorize things according to perceptual attributes (e.g., shapes and size), but rather develop meanings of early words based on their actions if they are animate objects, or on the objects performed on them if they are inanimate objects; children form concepts by viewing objects in terms of the whole, not a sum of parts or features.
Disorder in which there is a failure to identify a pathology of an organ system after using the best diagnostic procedures and technologies available.
Fillmore's theory that meaning comes not just from structure and grammar but from the semantic relationships between the words chosen, adding a deeper level to Chomsky's LAD.
A girl discovered in 1970 at age 13 after severe isolation and neglect; despite rehabilitation she never gained full grammatical competence — a key case for the critical-period hypothesis.
Verbal or nonfinite verb form (based on a verb and expresses action or a state of being) that ends in -ing and functions as a noun.
Repeating aloud what a child said while recording a sample, so the utterance can be understood later during transcription.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)
Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The space between the vocal folds.
When speakers delete or withhold information that they assume listeners already possess.
A morpheme (inflection or small function word) that signals grammatical relationships; Brown identified 14 that children acquire in a fairly predictable order.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

glossary.def: Ability to match letters to individual sounds.
Halliday's categorization of the purposes behind a child's communication into seven functions.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)
Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The bony front portion of the roof of the mouth.
Unrelated statements connected by a common originating stimulus where information is simply chained together in an additive fashion without a meaningful sequence.
Expectations teachers have for student behavior.
Adding semantic features to one's definitions of a word to create a greater understanding and use of a word in common situations with greater differentiation of it from other words.

Collective skills, knowledge, or other intangible assets of individuals that can be used to create economic value. These skills are influenced by culture and are affected by parent and societal beliefs about age, gender, and birth order.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A bone of the laryngeal region (U-shaped, in the neck) that supports the larynx and tongue musculature.
Commonly used combination of words that has a figurative meaning, which is separate from the literal meaning or definition of the actual words in the phrase (e.g., "The cat's out of the bag").
Purpose or motive underlying an utterance.
Time between 8 and about 12 months of age when infants begin to use gestures and combine these with vocalizations to express a range of specific and recognizable communicative functions.
Duplication of models one hears and sees.
Noun that refers to nonliving things.
Number of new cases of a disorder.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The middle ossicle, connecting the malleus to the stapes.

Readers who confidently and competently read on their own and when they are alone, pay little conscious attention to the details of printed words but rather focus on constructing and maintaining meaning.

Pragmatic feature of language referring to the circumstances or context in which a communicative message takes place; situational context is important in establishing meaning in our communicative attempts.
Expression of desire or inclination requiring the receiver of a request to use an inference (I am very thirsty).
Caregiver singing (e.g., lullabies) that soothes the infant and builds attachment by matching the caregiver's calming emotional state.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

glossary.def: Change in a word created by adding a grammatical morpheme.
Suffixes that change the meaning of words by marking grammatical adjustments for things such as plurality, possession, and verb tense.

Theory that examines the sequence and execution of cognitive events, focusing on how individuals attend, encode, relate, store, and retrieve information, particularly for language acquisition purposes.
Providing information.
Using language to tell someone something the speaker knows (or thinks they know) that the listener does not.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

glossary.def: Word or phrase that precedes a determiner and places a limit on the noun (only, all, both, just).

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: Sensory cells in the cochlea arranged by the tone/frequency of the sound they pick up; their stimulation generates the neural signal for hearing.
Reading level at which a reader quickly scans reading materials to determine the main ideas.
Teaching format that involves engaging, informal discussion about a designated topic between students and teacher in which ideas are explored.

Fourth and final stage of writing development in which writers develop a style that reflects their own personality, makes them unique, and allows them to express varying moods and attitudes in their writing; not all individuals will reach this stage.
Significant limitations in intelligence as determined by an IQ test score below 70, and limitations in adaptive behavior.
Degree to which speech can be understood.
A moderate view on the nature–nurture continuum holding that both biological and environmental factors matter and that language develops through the child's social interactions.
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Anything that people are able to hear, they are also able to reproduce through spoken language; Charles Hockett's fourth "design-feature" of language.
Type of language hybrid that combines rules from a dominant language, rules from a second language, and rules a child invents to bridge any gaps between the two.
Term to conceptualize the psychological relationship between individuals.
One of Skinner's verbal operants: social/conversational talk within a situational context.
Stage of spelling development in which young children use their best judgments about spelling words using visual memory and sounding-out strategies.

The initiate-response-evaluate (IRE) model of questioning; a traditional teacher-directed question-and-answer session to check for factual knowledge or fast recall whereby the teacher initiates a question, the student responds, and the teacher then evaluates the answer.
Negative statement intended to mean something positive.
Positive statement with the intent to mean something negative.
Use of words to express something other than or opposite to the literal meaning.
Verb form that indicates an action took place in the past, but does not follow conventional past tense (-ed) morphology rules (e.g., ran, sat).
The theorist behind classical conditioning; contributor to behaviorism.
Babbling that imitates adult-like speech patterns in intonation, stress, and rhythm; may mix with true words into toddlerhood.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

glossary.def: Final stage of babbling, also known as conversational babbling, in which productions are distinguished by melodic patterns and have many of the characteristics of real speech such as rhythm, stress, rate variations, and intonational contours.
A cognitive theorist who held that language development mirrors (follows from) cognitive development, beginning in the sensorimotor period.
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: The primary theorist of the social interactionist view; proposed the LASS and emphasized caregiver interaction in language learning.
A philosopher who, with Searle, developed speech act theory (the pragmatics revolution).
A philosopher who, with Austin, developed speech act theory (the pragmatics revolution).
Shared focus of two individuals (e.g., caregiver and child) on each other or on an object or event; joint reference.
Sharing the same focus of attention with a caregiver (begins ~2 months); requires shared eye contact and following eye-gaze or pointing. Sets the stage for language (also called joint attention).
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

glossary.def: A bonobo (pygmy chimpanzee) who acquired symbols by exposure rather than direct teaching and showed some sensitivity to word order.
glossary.source: Born to Talk, Ch. 2: Language Acquisition — A Theoretical Journey

glossary.def: System of arbitrary, established symbols and rule-governed structures used for communication that change over time; conventionalized sounds, signs, gestures, or symbols that have shared and understood meanings.
Concept of the nativist theory of language that humans are born with the innate "device" for acquiring language.
Bruner's concept of the social support structure — caregiver interaction and scaffolding — that supports language acquisition; the social counterpart to Chomsky's LAD.

glossary.term: Language of academic subjects or curriculum
glossary.def: Specific vocabulary and manners of discourse associated with education and academics.
Traditional type of language used by teachers to establish who is allowed to talk, what one is allowed to say, and how one is allowed to say it in a classroom environment.
Language that is necessary for people to express themselves to others and develop a sense of self.
A recorded (usually audio/video) and transcribed sample of all the language a child produces during an interaction, analyzed across syntax, grammar, semantics, and pragmatics.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)
Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The raw buzzing sound produced by vocal-fold vibration before it is shaped by resonation into recognizable speech sounds.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The 'voice box.' Its primary function is protecting the trachea and lungs from foreign material; its secondary function is sound production. Built from cartilages — most importantly the thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis, and arytenoids.
The upper range of Brown's Stage I (MLU ~1.5-2.0): emerging two-word combinations.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

glossary.def: Idea that learning occurs when people's innate capacity for learning, a learning environment, and some stimulus for learning that comes from learners themselves are combined, suggesting that cognitive structures interact with experience to produce learning.

Broad term used to designate difficulties in acquiring spoken language, written language, and mathematical skills; disorder is presumed to be due to neurological causes and not due to other causes, such as sensory loss, motor conditions, environment, and cultural differences.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The cerebral hemisphere where primary speech and language functions originate for most people.
Visual acuity that is 20/200 or less in the better eye, or having a 20-degree visual field.
Third stage of spelling development in which a child represents vowels as well as consonants with letters whose names sound like the speech sounds they are assumed to represent.
A social-interactionist theorist who emphasized that social interaction drives development; originated the Zone of Proximal Development.
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Theory that children have the innate ability to acquire one language completely, but do not have the ability to acquire two or more languages simultaneously without suffering some reduction in competence in one or both languages.
Structural features and rules shared by all human languages, taken by nativists as evidence that language is part of human biology.
glossary.source: Born to Talk, Ch. 2: Language Acquisition — A Theoretical Journey

glossary.def: Level of reading at which a student focuses on word meanings and the relationships between ideas conveyed in the paragraph.
Producing an utterance using words via speaking, signing, or using assistive technology.
Time around 12 months and older when a child begins using words to communicate.
Organization of narrative information or components into a temporal order of related ideas.
A researcher who stressed the role of context — both linguistic and non-linguistic information — in understanding child language.
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Some functional use of eyesight ranging from a moderate to severe impairment.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: Passive structures in the thorax that receive air — they do not actively 'suck in' air; airflow results from pressure changes governed by Boyle's Law.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The first ossicle, attached to the eardrum; it is set into motion first, then vibrates the incus.
One of Skinner's verbal operants: requesting.
Description of how a consonant sound is produced, such as a stop, fricative, or nasal.
Early form of babbling in which an infant strings together single consonants and vowels that are made in a row, such as "a, a, a," and "da, da, da."
Sounds that occur less frequently in languages of the world and develop later because they are more difficult to produce.
Sounds that a child can consistently produce accurately.
Relating to science or learning.
Using language for the function of learning about the world.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

glossary.def: Calculation of the average number of morphemes a child produces in a representative sample of utterances.
The average number of morphemes per utterance; a common measure of a child's syntactic/grammatical development (Brown).
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

glossary.def: Conceptual extension of causality; the understanding that there are ways (means) to attain a goal (end).
Using cause and effect to determine the means (actions) that achieve an end (goal), whether through actions or words; a key sensorimotor skill.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

glossary.def: Ability to think about the language and manipulate the components of language, such as counting syllables and sounds in words.
A network of mirror neurons implicated in imitation; differences in the MNS have been linked to autism spectrum disorder.
glossary.source: Born to Talk, Ch. 2: Language Acquisition — A Theoretical Journey

glossary.def: Specialized neurons whose activity has been found to represent actions that can be used not only for imitating actions but also to recognize and determine differences in the actions of others; neurons that "mirror" the behavior of others, as though the observer itself were acting. It has been proposed that problems with the mirror neural system may underlie cognitive disorders, particularly in children with autism.
Combination of conductive and sensorineural hearing loss.
Type of auxiliary verb used to indicate the attitude or mood of the verb that it precedes (e.g., must, will, should).
Characteristics of sentences such as verb tense or the expression of negation or interrogation.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The cone-shaped bone at the core of the cochlea around which the nerve pathways spiral; it connects to the auditory nerve.
Children learn to expand on noun and verb phrases in order to create distinct meanings with words in sentences.
Smallest grammatical unit in a language that conveys meaning.
The study of morphemes: how word parts combine to build words and convey grammatical meaning.
glossary.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Speech sound change that occurs when the shape of the base morpheme is changed (e.g., the final sound in the word public is the k sound, but when public becomes publicity, that k becomes an s sound).
General style used by adults when talking to young children, often characterized by higher pitch, a "cooing" intonation, and simplified or shortened words.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The brain region that sends signals to the speech mechanism to produce the speech that represents the formulated language.
Idea that all students regardless of gender, race, culture, social class, religion, or exceptionality should experience educational equality in the school.
Voice disorder in which the larynx is strained due to inappropriate or excessive use of the muscles above and around the vocal folds.

Brief period during which a child (typically 18-20 months) experiences short-term difficulty with word recall. Thought to occur due to the densely packed representations stored in memory during rapid vocabulary growth which produces competition in word selection, or because the child's words are undergoing reorganization, causing confusion about words that have strong semantic relationships.
A story; an account of events or experiences.
Type of written or verbal communication that involves telling a story, typically involving a sequential order of events.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The nose cavity; a resonating chamber, coupled or sealed off from the vocal tract by the velum.
The theory that language is innate and biologically based (an argument for NATURE); humans are pre-wired to acquire language.
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Sounds common to all languages and emerge first in developing children.
The position that development is driven primarily by genetics/biology — we are 'born this way.'
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Removing something desirable after a behavior to decrease it (e.g., no video games for not finishing homework).
Removing something undesirable after a behavior to increase that behavior (e.g., extending bedtime for finishing homework). Note: 'negative' = removed, not 'bad.'
Variety of conditions related to muscle control and innervations of the muscles involved in respiration, phonation, resonation, and articulation.
The linguist most associated with nativism, generative grammar, and the LAD; argued all humans acquire language.
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: An object is expected to be present or occur, but is not, or an action is expected to occur, but does not; words used to express this relationship may be all gone or no.
Group of words containing a noun and words that describe or modify the noun.
The position that development is driven primarily by environment and experience.
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Words that refer to things receiving action.
Knowledge that objects exist in time and space even if you can't see or act on them.
Semantic relation of using and to connect a clause that describes or elaborates on the subject of the preceding clause; linking subjects and objects appropriately in a listing sense.
Personal pronoun that acts as the object of a sentence and receives the action of the verb (e.g., me, her, him, them).
A context in which Standard English requires a particular morpheme; a morpheme is considered mastered when used correctly in ~90% of its obligatory contexts.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

glossary.def: Words that can be used alone and in combination with other open words, in combination with pivot words, and in either the first or second position of two-word utterances.
Any behavior whereby frequency can be affected by the responses following it.
Learning in which behavior is shaped by its consequences — reinforcement increases behavior, punishment decreases it.
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck
Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The mouth; a resonating cavity whose shape is changed (by tongue, jaw, and lips) to alter the sound produced.

When a child learning language interprets a sentence according to the order of the phrases, rather than the meaning of the phrases; concept that in the normal thought process, a cause is identified before its effect is considered.
Disorder caused by a demonstrable pathology of an organ system.
Natural tendency of the mind to organize information into related, interconnected structures, with a scheme being the most basic structure.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The chain of three tiny bones in the middle ear — malleus, incus, and stapes — that transmit eardrum vibration to the inner ear.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The oval-shaped opening into which the stapes footplate fits; its motion sets the inner-ear fluids moving.
When a child uses a word or concept too broadly (e.g., calling all four-legged animals "doggie").
The simplified, exaggerated, and repetitive speech register caregivers use with infants and young children (child-directed speech).
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Changing the surface structure of a sentence so that the grammatical subject receives the verb's action; example: "The ball was hit by the boy."
Processes by which an individual selects, organizes, integrates, and interprets sensory stimuli.
The actual production and use of language, as distinct from the underlying competence.
glossary.source: Born to Talk, Ch. 2: Language Acquisition — A Theoretical Journey
Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The cranial and spinal nerves that carry speech and language messages out to the muscles. Includes 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.
Effect a locutionary act might have on a listener, which may or may not be consistent with the speaker's communicative intention.

Time between birth and about 8 months of age during which infants respond in a reflexive manner to their environment and are not signaling any communication intent other than crying and nonspecific use of face and body.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The throat cavity; one of the three resonating cavities that shape the laryngeal tone.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The second subsystem of speech: the production of sound at the larynx. Biological function is airway protection; speech function is generating the raw laryngeal (glottal) tone.
Speech sound; the smallest contrastive unit in the sound system of a particular language.
Ability to focus on and understand the sound structure of language.

Underlying disorder in establishing and using the appropriate rules for sounds and their combinations, characterized by difficulty mastering where to use speech sounds in order to make words sound different from each other.

Human ability to process rapidly paced speech and impose a phonemic (sound) identity to incoming speech sounds which are then analyzed, the structure of words is determined, and the code for each word is stored, along with its meaning, in long-term, semantic memory.
A working-memory storage system for the temporary holding of verbal messages and information (for long-term memory or speech).
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

glossary.def: The stored sound pattern that represents a word; hearing the word later lets us retrieve the thing or concept associated with it.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

glossary.def: Study of speech sounds and the rules that determine how sounds can be sequenced into syllables and words in a language.
The rules that specify how sounds can be combined within a language.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

glossary.def: Rules that govern the permissible arrangements of sounds in a given language.
Combination of words that are related to one another and that serves a grammatical purpose, but does not contain both a subject and a predicate.
Universal rules for all languages, associated with Chomsky's transformational grammar, that describe the underlying relationships of words and phrases.

Language that usually develops for the purpose of allowing groups with different languages to trade or communicate, and includes a combination of both languages, beginning as an informal language consisting mostly of nouns and many gestures and eventually becoming more formal.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The visible ear on the outside of the head; it helps direct sound into the ear canal.

Words that cannot be used alone or combined with other pivot words but can be used in conjunction with almost any other word a child has learned, and are used in either the first or second position of two-word utterances.
Proposed primitive form of grammar which suggests that children have two classes of words: open and pivot; concept used to explain the structure behind two-word phrases often used by children.
Point of contact where an obstruction occurs in the vocal tract when producing a consonant, helping to give a consonant its distinctive sound.
Dynamic flexibility and adaptability of the human brain to change—physically, functionally, and chemically throughout life, and as individuals constantly learn.
Child-directed activities that provide children with opportunities for learning.
Noun form used to denote that there are two or more of something.
Adding something undesirable after a behavior to decrease it (e.g., extra chores for not finishing homework).
Adding something desirable after a behavior to increase that behavior (e.g., video-game time for finishing homework).
Noun form used to denote ownership, marked by adding an 's to the end of a noun, or an apostrophe after plural nouns.
Adjective phrase that comes after a noun ("The man who called last night is my uncle").
Minimum level of income based on the size of the family unit and updated each year by the U.S. Census Bureau to use for statistical estimates of the number of Americans living in poverty.
Using language to get something done.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

glossary.def: Component of language regarding the ability to functionally use language in social contexts; the rules for social language needed to establish and maintain relationships with others.
The interactionist view that language is produced with an outcome in mind; associated with Austin and Searle and analyzed through speech acts.
Early turn-taking imitation (substage 2): the infant does a behavior, an adult imitates it back, and the infant imitates in return; sets the stage for later play.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

glossary.def: A morpheme added to the beginning of a word (e.g., 're-' in 'replay').
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

glossary.def: Piaget's second stage (2 to 7 years); rapid language growth and learning through hands-on visual/motor tasks, but egocentric thinking and one-dimensional problem solving.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

glossary.def: First stage of writing development in which a child is learning to form letters.
First stage of spelling development in which children scribble, inconsistently form letters, and string letters together with little awareness that letters represent phonemes or speech sounds.
Verb form that indicates an action is taking place right now.
Assumption that speakers make concerning what their listener knows about the subject of their conversation.
Total number of cases of a disorder/disease in a population at a particular time.
Ability of humans to intentionally deceive others in their communications.
Verb that usually accompanies or helps the main verb by expressing or making distinctions in mood, voice, aspect, and tense.
Area in the frontal lobe of the brain, also known as the precentral gyrus or primary motor cortex, involved in the planning and execution of motor movements, including swallowing and speech.
Child's use of a word, a change in prosodic pattern, or a gesture to communicate.

Dore's categorization of one-word-stage communication into distinct purposes (e.g., labeling, answering, requesting an action, requesting an answer, calling, greeting, protesting, repeating, practicing).
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

glossary.def: Concept that the preceding noun closest to the verb is treated as the subject of the sentence.
A child's realization that oral language can be represented by print, or written language.
During reading, when a caregiver highlights and points out basic elements of print to direct a child's attention to the forms, features, and functions of written language.

Knowledge of the rule-governed organizational properties of print, including being able to show the front of the book, the title, the difference between pictures and print, left-to-right and top-to-bottom directionality for reading, and the concepts of letter and first letter in a word.

Vygotsky's term for the self-talk people use to direct their actions, learning, planning, and problem-solving. It starts out loud in childhood, becomes whispered with age, and is eventually internalized as inner thought.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

glossary.def: Human ability to create an infinite variety of novel and unique messages from a previously existing finite collection of sounds; Charles Hockett's 11th "design-feature" of language.
Word that takes the place of a noun or noun phrase.
Characteristics of a sentence such as the relationship between nouns and verbs; the content of a meaningful, declarative sentence.
Primitive speech act used to establish social interaction and direct a caregiver's attention; use of a gesture (sometimes paired with a vocalization) to gain attention to an object or event.
Bates' term for pointing that establishes joint attention by directing attention to things of interest.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

glossary.def: Primitive speech act used as a request for objects or actions as well as to control and manipulate the behaviors of others.
Bates' term for pointing/gesturing used to have demands met or to control others. (Lack of pointing ~12 months can be a red flag for autism.)
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

glossary.def: Young children's early recounts or storytelling in temporal-causal sequences.

Idea that children rely on both perceptual features and functions of words to develop early meanings; children build mental models of a conceptual category—an ideal or representative example (prototype) that other members of this group must resemble.
Popular, wise saying or a precise statement of truth.
Onset of stuttering associated with a specific, identifiable psychological trauma.
Hoarseness or complete loss of the voice without physical cause, but rather due to severe emotional trauma or conflict.
Consequence used to cause a behavior to occur with less frequency.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A special pathway of the central nervous system controlling refined, intricate movements of structures such as the lips and tongue (the articulators).
Sounds that have a low pitch and a muffled resonance quality (e.g., grunting, crying, reflexive fussing, and vegetative sounds).
Speech signals are transitory and a listener can only receive specific auditory information at the time it is spoken; Charles Hockett's third "design-feature" of language.
Listening to and understanding what is communicated; the ability to comprehend a message.
The narration or telling of past events or experiences.
When an object reappears or an event happens again; words used to express this relationship may be more or another.

Human ability to use acquired knowledge to create language, imagine what others may be thinking, engage in mental time travel to the past and the future, think about and gain understanding of self, and to relate to a divine being in the development and demonstration of spirituality.
More specific term for babbling involving repeated consonant-vowel (CV) syllables (e.g., "mamama").
Human ability to use language to think and talk about language; also referred to as metalinguistic ability.
A Hockett design feature: language can be used to talk about language itself.
glossary.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: A variety of language used by people living in a restricted geographic area and distinguished by features of vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation from other regional variations.
Verb form that indicates an action took place in the past (e.g., danced, looked).
Consequence used to cause a behavior to occur with greater frequency.
Words that indicate relationships among people, objects, and events; these words reflect a child's understanding of space, time, amount, dimensions, and kinship.
Pertinence, timeliness, or usefulness of a conversational topic.
The degree to which a language sample is a true, representative capture of the child's typical abilities (not skewed by, e.g., shyness that day).
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

glossary.def: Ability to think about things or use words without having to act on them directly.
Signify some features of an object or its function; have meaning independent of the objects (e.g., holding a fist to the ear to mean "telephone").

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The third subsystem of speech: the laryngeal tone is shaped by the size and shape of the pharynx, oral, and nasal cavities. Plays its most important role in shaping vowel sounds (open sounds with free airflow).

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The first subsystem of speech. Biologically it is breathing (O2/CO2 exchange); for speech it provides the 'power' — the airstream that drives sound production. Breathing for life is ~50% inhalation / 50% exhalation; breathing for speech is ~15% inhalation / 85% exhalation (controlled, extended exhalation up to ~15 seconds).
When a preceding sound affects a sound that follows.

Student-led format in which a teacher facilitates learning by promoting student discussion, acknowledging responses, and posing questions to prompt further thought; repeating part or all of a student's utterance or response and asking the student to verify whether the interpretation is correct.
Using context to help determine the meanings of a child's utterances.
The base part of a word that carries its core meaning, to which prefixes and suffixes attach.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

glossary.def: Perceptual relevance; a pronounced feature.
Support given during the learning process that is tailored to the needs of the individual and gradually removed to promote independent learning.
Cognitive structure that helps children process, identify, organize, and store information.

Conceptualized rules about who talks to whom and when these interactions should occur in a classroom environment, as well as the attitudes and values of teachers regarding the expectations of how to use language in the classroom.

Interconnected neural system, in which learning in one language domain, such as the sound system, cannot help but affect other language domains, such as grammar; network involved in the learning, storing, organizing, and retrieving of information.
Proactive and self-directed process of writing in which a writer takes into account aspects such as the audience and the literary style most appropriate to convey the message.
Idea that the order of appearance of words in the course of a child's language acquisition is governed by the type and complexity of the semantic features they contain.
An interactionist view that shifts emphasis from structure to meaning in explaining language.
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Underlying rules for combining words and grammar to produce meaningful utterances; concept that emphasizes that meaning precedes and influences form.

Ability to use human speech to convey particular messages, and the idea that speech is needed in most cases to ensure the specificity of messages; Charles Hockett's seventh "design-feature" of language.
Component of language regarding the meaning and interpretation of language; the use of vocabulary to construct ideas through relationships between words.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The inner-ear structures responsible for balance.
Piaget's first stage of intellectual development (birth to 2 years); knowledge is built through the senses and motor action, and it is prerequisite to language development. Broken into 6 substages.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

glossary.def: Piaget's first stage of cognitive development (birth–2 years), when symbolic play parallels the child's realization that words stand for people, places, and things.
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Hearing loss caused by damage to the auditory nervous system, due to heredity, infection, trauma, exposure to toxins, or repeated exposure to loud noise. The damage may be located in the cochlea of the inner ear, the auditory nerve, various points along the auditory pathway, or in the primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe of the brain.

Grammatical unit consisting of one or more words meaningfully grouped to express a statement, question, exclamation, request, command, or suggestion; a grammatical unit consisting of a noun and verb phrase.
The cognitive ability to order objects by a property such as size; Piaget argued a child must reach this stage before using comparative adjectives like 'bigger.'
Changing the topic of conversation by deriving a new topic from the immediately previous topic so that some continuity in the conversational flow is maintained.
Tendency of young children learning common nouns to generalize on the basis of shape, rather than material, color, or texture.
Developing a behavior through small steps that gradually approximate the target behavior.
Rhythmic characteristic of motherese, which is more regular than adult speech, resulting in what some researchers describe as a singsong cadence.
Process by which a child learns two languages at once during early childhood.
Building deeper, fuller word meaning over time through repeated exposure to a word in varied contexts.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

glossary.def: Gradual process over time of expanding, reorganizing, and fine-tuning word meanings as words are acquired and the relationship between words develops along with cognition and linguistic attainments.

Educational strategy that leads students, through their increased understanding of cultural diversity, to make decisions about how best to address social issues affected by cultural differences and encouraging students to actually take action to solve problems that are created by cultural differences.

Explanation of language acquisition in which both environmental and biological factors are important in the process; however, the role of social interaction between the developing child and linguistically knowledgeable adults is emphasized.
An interactionist view emphasizing that children interact socially before producing language and that language develops from those interactions; focuses on language USE (pragmatics).
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Resources available to individuals based on group membership, relationships inside and outside of the group, and networks of influence and support in combination with access to forms of knowledge, skills, education, advantages, and attitudes necessary to gain social and economic mobility.
Nonfinancial social assets that promote social mobility beyond economic means (e.g., education, intellect, dress).
Expected combined or economic benefits taken from the preferential treatment and cooperation between individuals and groups.
Position of an individual on a hierarchical social-economic scale that measures factors such as education, income, type of occupation, and place of residence.
Fluctuation of pressure passed through some medium (e.g., air or water), composed of frequencies within the range of hearing.

Idea that speech is a specialized human function (made apparent by the anatomy of human speech organs and the human ability to exhibit some control over these organs), is specifically designed for communication, and serves no other purpose; Charles Hockett's sixth "design-feature" of language.
Term used to categorize a childhood language disorder that is not accompanied by deficits in hearing, intelligence, neurological, or motor function.
Oral expression of language.
The theory that utterances perform acts, analyzed as locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts.
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck
Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The 31 pairs of nerves that, among other roles, are responsible for controlling respiration.
Variety of a language spoken by people of relatively high status who have economic, political, social, and educational power.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The third ossicle; its footplate fits into the oval window, moving the fluids of the inner ear.
Knowledge about general structure of stories and how to ask oneself important questions while reading stories to facilitate comprehension.

Speech disorder characterized by disruptions in the flow of speech by involuntary repetitions and prolongations of sounds, syllables, words, or phrases as well as involuntary silent pauses or blocks in which sound is unable to be produced.
Personal pronoun (e.g., I, he, she, they) that acts as the subject of the sentence and performs the action of the verb.
Words that refer to objects or events that have perceptual or functional features in common (e.g., doggie, horsie, truck).
Form of language simplification in which children use phonemes within their developmental level as substitutes for sounds they are not able to use consistently.
Environment in which children who speak a minority language give up their minority language when acquiring the majority language, and in this process, give up their culture.
The consecutive development of two or more languages.
A morpheme added to the end of a word, which can change its category (e.g., '-er' in 'teacher').
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

glossary.def: Adjective used to compare three or more nouns, occurs through the addition of the suffix -est.
Features of speech, such as stress, pitch, and duration, that accompany individual speech sounds, words, and sentences.
In Chomsky's transformational grammar, the outward form of a sentence, which is derived from deep structures by a series of transformations.
Arrangement of vowels and consonants that make up a single syllable.
A play activity in which objects or actions are used to represent other objects and actions.

Change in a child's processing and organization of words to reflect more adultlike patterns of organizing words into classes, rather than by syntactic relationships (e.g., syntagmatic relationship: "cat-meows"; paradigmatic relationship: "cat-animal").
Rules that govern the ways in which words combine to form phrases, clauses, and sentences; sentence structure.
One of Skinner's verbal operants: labeling — verbal behavior associated with a thing or action.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A membrane within the cochlea whose movement (from fluid motion) triggers the inner hair cells.
Simplified manner of speech during the early years of language acquisition using the most important content words for expressing ideas lacking appropriate grammar and inflection.
Expresses aspects and relations of time to discuss one event that follows another in time.
The chain of events connecting a speaker's brain to a listener's brain during communication, moving through linguistic, physiological, and acoustic levels and back.
glossary.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Cognitive ability to designate mental states—beliefs, intents, desires, knowledge, and so on—to oneself and others, and to understand that others have different mental states than oneself.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The chest cavity containing the lungs, diaphragm, and 12 thoracic vertebrae, caged in by 12 pairs of ribs. Changes in its volume drive breathing.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The outer cartilage of the larynx, which may protrude as the 'Adam's apple.' The vocal folds attach to it.
Strategy whereby one conversational partner matches the topic of the other conversational partner.

Story that connects two or more different events that share a common theme, in which each episode in the narrative might have different characters, and the stories might occur in different places and times.
Story centered on single characters or on single events having clearly defined chronologies.

Speakers have the ability to hear themselves speak, and through this, receive feedback allowing them to make constant adjustments so that output is as finely tuned as possible for conveying accurate thoughts. This feedback also provides control for the mechanics of speech so that speech errors are caught and corrected or even anticipated and avoided; Charles Hockett's fifth "design-feature" of language.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The windpipe; the tube through which exhaled air passes up from the lungs toward the larynx.

Idea that speech is instinctive in humans and the capacity for language acquisition is genetic; however, the details of a language, including vocabulary and structural rules, are learned; Charles Hockett's 13th and last "design-feature" of language.

Education strategy that fundamentally changes an existing curriculum by redesigning it to allow students to understand, appreciate, and value concepts, issues, events, and themes from the perspectives of a representative range of ethnic and cultural groups.

Linguistic theory, developed by Noam Chomsky, that attempts to account for the infinite number of grammatical sentences possible in a language. This theory suggests that language is processed at two levels, deep and surface.
Nonuniversal rules or conventions that describe a language's deep structure and surface structure.
Around 5 months: the transition from cooing into single-syllable vowel and consonant sounds.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

glossary.def: Fourth and last stage of spelling development in which children may try a number of spelling strategies including using a particular spelling they saw in print, applying rules for spelling they observed, and continuing to rely on letter-name spellings and sounding-out strategies to spell words.
Sudden trauma to the brain that causes injury.
Stories that focus on a true plot, character development, a sequence of events, and a definite resolution of the central conflict or problem.
The meaning relationships a child expresses by combining two words (e.g., agent+action, action+object, possessor+possession); typical of Brown's Stage I.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)
Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The eardrum, located at the end of the ear canal; it absorbs sound energy and vibrates, passing that vibration to the ossicles.
The number of different words divided by the total number of words in a sample; a measure of vocabulary diversity (~0.5 for young children).
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

glossary.def: The natural, automatic reaction to an unconditioned stimulus.
A stimulus that naturally and automatically triggers a response without any learning.
When a child uses a word too narrowly (e.g., only calling golden retrievers "doggie"); not applying a new word to things that are included in the meaning of that word.
Styles of language used during the school day appropriate for interactions with peers.

Concept that children who are exposed to two languages from birth in the first stage of language development, actually function with a single language that is a hybrid of two distinctly different languages, a hybrid that includes vocabulary and grammatical rules from both languages.
Typically one thought, often signaled by a pause; the unit segmented and counted in language-sample analysis.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

glossary.def: The degree to which an assessment or sample actually measures what it is supposed to measure.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

glossary.def: More complex form of babbling involving more complex combinations of consonant and vowel syllables (e.g., "madagaba").

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The soft, muscular back portion of the roof of the mouth. It moves up and back to close the mouth off from the nasal cavity, directing airflow.
Group of words that contains a verb and possibly other supporting or qualifying words.
Native, nonstandard variety of language from a specific population.
Developing an understanding of the deeper meanings of words by taking a known word and breaking it down into categories.
Grammatical over-generalizations (e.g., 'drinked' for 'drank') that show a child is actively applying rules, not merely imitating; also called intelligent mistakes.
A working-memory storage system that lets us create and adjust mental images.
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

glossary.def: Consistent patterns of sounds, unique to individual children, used in reference to particular things or situations; also referred to as phonetically consistent forms, performatives, or protowords.
The period of rapid vocabulary growth (roughly 18–20 months), associated with the temporary naming deficit.
glossary.source: Born to Talk, Ch. 2: Language Acquisition — A Theoretical Journey
Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: Paired structures of muscle and ligament that attach to the thyroid cartilage and to the arytenoids. Their rapid opening and closing (vibration) in the airstream produces the laryngeal tone.
Process by which infants "play" and experiment with their voices by changing the loudness, pitch, rate, and quality (e.g., squeals, grunts, raspberries).

Idea that standard human language occurs as a vocal type of communication in which air is forced through the vocal folds of the larynx, breaking the vibrating air stream into sounds of speech, which are organized into words and sentences and perceived through a listener's ears; Charles Hockett's first "design-feature" of language.
The vocal quality produced at the larynx — pitch, loudness, and resonance/quality.
glossary.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

glossary.def: Use of vocal fold vibration to produce all vowel sounds and certain consonant sounds.
