Simplification of vowel sounds due to a child's tendency to produce vowels in the center of the oral cavity, making it neither high-low nor front-back, which results in vowels that are either too high or low or made too far in front or back of the intended target; a process more common for children with hearing loss.
A chimpanzee taught American Sign Language by the Gardners; learned 100+ signs and combined them, but showed no consistent grammatical rules.
glossary.source: Born to Talk, Ch. 2: Language Acquisition — A Theoretical Journey
Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A left-hemisphere region responsible for language comprehension and formulation.
Idea that the organizing principle in early phonological development is whole words, not features or segments.
The roughly 30-million-word difference in language exposure by age 3 between children from the wealthiest vs. poorest families (low-income ~616 words/hr vs. professional ~2,153 words/hr).
glossary.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

glossary.def: Ability to recall stored information, or known words, from long-term memory.
Process of creating a permanent record of encoded information of a specific word in memory.
System that actively holds and allows for the voluntary, focused, and exclusive processing and maintenance of task-relevant information.
Range of abilities a child can perform with assistance, but cannot yet perform independently.
Vygotsky's concept: the gap between what a child can do independently and what they can do with guidance/support.
glossary.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: What are the four processes (subsystems) of speech, in order?
flashcards.back: Respiration → Phonation → Resonation → Articulation.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Respiration: bio function vs. speech function?
flashcards.back: Bio: breathing / gas exchange. Speech: provides the 'power' (the airstream).
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Breathing ratio for life vs. for speech?
flashcards.back: Life ≈ 50% inhalation / 50% exhalation. Speech ≈ 15% inhalation / 85% exhalation (controlled exhalation up to ~15 sec).
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: State Boyle's Law.
flashcards.back: At constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional (constant product). Volume up → pressure down → air rushes in; volume down → pressure up → air flows out.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: What is the primary muscle of inhalation, and what happens when it contracts?
flashcards.back: The diaphragm. It flattens from its resting dome shape, enlarging the thorax (volume up, pressure down) so air is forced into the lungs.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Phonation: bio function vs. speech function?
flashcards.back: Bio: airway protection. Speech: produces sound (the laryngeal tone).
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Name the four most important laryngeal cartilages.
flashcards.back: Thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis, and arytenoids.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Which cartilage is the 'Adam's apple'?
flashcards.back: The thyroid cartilage (outer cartilage of the larynx).
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: What is the glottis?
flashcards.back: The space between the vocal folds.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Adductors vs. abductors of the vocal folds?
flashcards.back: Adductors bring the folds together (close the glottis); abductors move them apart (open the glottis).
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: List the 5 steps of the phonation cycle.
flashcards.back: 1) Adduction of the vocal folds. 2) Exhaled air pressure builds beneath the adducted folds. 3) Pressure blows the folds apart, releasing a puff of air. 4) Sub-fold pressure drops. 5) Reduced pressure + fold elasticity snaps them back together — cycle repeats.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: How many phonation cycles per second in males vs. females?
flashcards.back: Males: ~120–145 per second. Females: ~200–260 per second.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Resonation: which cavities shape the tone, and what does it shape most?
flashcards.back: Pharynx, oral, and nasal cavities. Shapes vowel sounds most importantly.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Articulation is most associated with shaping which speech sounds?
flashcards.back: Consonant sounds.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Name the articulators.
flashcards.back: Teeth, tongue, lips, alveolar ridge, hard palate, soft palate (velum), and jaw.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Where is the alveolar ridge?
flashcards.back: The hard, bumpy ridge directly behind the top front teeth.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Broca's area vs. Wernicke's area?
flashcards.back: Broca's = motor planning/coordination of articulation. Wernicke's = language comprehension and formulation.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: What does the arcuate fasciculus do?
flashcards.back: Transmits language information, connecting Wernicke's area to Broca's area.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Pyramidal vs. extrapyramidal system?
flashcards.back: Pyramidal controls refined, intricate movements (lips, tongue / articulators). Extrapyramidal controls gross, unskilled motor movements.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: How many pairs of cranial nerves and spinal nerves? Roles?
flashcards.back: 12 pairs of cranial nerves (6 primarily for motor speech) and 31 pairs of spinal nerves (control respiration).
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: What are the three parts of the ear?
flashcards.back: Outer, middle, and inner ear.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Name the three ossicles in order from eardrum inward.
flashcards.back: Malleus (hammer) → incus (anvil) → stapes (stirrup).
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Which structure fits into the oval window, and what does that cause?
flashcards.back: The stapes footplate; it moves the fluids of the inner ear.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Inner ear: which structure handles hearing vs. balance?
flashcards.back: Cochlea = hearing. Semicircular canals = balance.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Trace the hearing pathway from eardrum to brain.
flashcards.back: Tympanic membrane → ossicles (malleus→incus→stapes) → oval window → cochlear fluids → tectorial membrane → inner hair cells → auditory nerve → brain.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Nativism argues for which side of the nature–nurture debate?
flashcards.back: NATURE — language is innate and biologically based.
flashcards.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: Who is the figurehead of nativism, and what did he claim?
flashcards.back: Noam Chomsky — 'all humans acquire language'; proposed the LAD.
flashcards.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: What is the Language Acquisition Device (LAD)?
flashcards.back: Chomsky's innate mental mechanism holding the universal rules of language that lets a child acquire any language they're exposed to.
flashcards.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: Behaviorism argues for which side of the debate, and by what mechanism?
flashcards.back: NURTURE — language is a learned behavior acquired through operant conditioning (Skinner).
flashcards.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: What does the 'empty vessel' analogy represent?
flashcards.back: The behaviorist idea that the child's mind is a blank container the environment fills with language.
flashcards.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: What is the interactionist position?
flashcards.back: A moderate view: both biology and environment matter, and language develops through the child's social interactions with caregivers.
flashcards.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: Vygotsky is known for which key concept?
flashcards.back: The Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) — the gap between what a child can do alone vs. with guidance.
flashcards.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: How does Piaget relate language to cognition?
flashcards.back: Language development mirrors cognitive development; it emerges during the sensorimotor period (birth–2).
flashcards.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: Name the three interactionist views.
flashcards.back: Semantic view, cognitive view, and social interactionist view.
flashcards.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: Semantic view: whose grammar, and what determines structure?
flashcards.back: Fillmore's case grammar — structure is dictated by the semantic relationship of verb and nouns (Bloom emphasized context).
flashcards.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: What does the cognitive view claim about language?
flashcards.back: Language is neither innate nor learned; it parallels cognitive development (Piaget; Information Processing Theory).
flashcards.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: What does the social interactionist view focus on?
flashcards.back: Language USE — pragmatics; social interaction precedes and drives language, supported by parentese.
flashcards.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: Name the three acts in Speech Act Theory.
flashcards.back: Locutionary (the utterance), illocutionary (the intended function), perlocutionary (the effect on the listener).
flashcards.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: In transformational generative grammar, what are the two levels?
flashcards.back: Deep structure (underlying, universal, from phrase structure rules) and surface structure (the actual form after transformations, language-specific).
flashcards.source: Born to Talk, Ch. 2: Language Acquisition — A Theoretical Journey

flashcards.front: Competence vs. performance?
flashcards.back: Competence = underlying knowledge of the language's rules; performance = actual use/production. Nativists stress competence.
flashcards.source: Born to Talk, Ch. 2: Language Acquisition — A Theoretical Journey

flashcards.front: Linguistic universals are used as evidence for which theory?
flashcards.back: Nativism — shared rules across all languages suggest language is part of human biology.
flashcards.source: Born to Talk, Ch. 2: Language Acquisition — A Theoretical Journey

flashcards.front: What did Washoe demonstrate, and what was the key limitation?
flashcards.back: A chimp learned 100+ ASL signs and combined them, but showed no consistent grammar/syntax.
flashcards.source: Born to Talk, Ch. 2: Language Acquisition — A Theoretical Journey

flashcards.front: What made Kanzi notable?
flashcards.back: A bonobo who acquired symbols by exposure (not direct teaching) and showed some comprehension of word order.
flashcards.source: Born to Talk, Ch. 2: Language Acquisition — A Theoretical Journey

flashcards.front: What are mirror neurons?
flashcards.back: Neurons that fire both when an individual performs an action and when they observe that action; theorized to support imitation and speech/language development.
flashcards.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: What is brain plasticity?
flashcards.back: The brain's ability to change and adapt its structure and function in response to experience.
flashcards.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: What is the self-organizing neural network?
flashcards.back: The brain's storage/filing system for words — how it organizes and retrieves vocabulary in memory.
flashcards.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: Receptive vs. expressive language?
flashcards.back: Receptive = comprehension (listening, reading). Expressive = production (speaking, writing, signing, AAC).
flashcards.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: Communication framework: name the SPEECH components and the LANGUAGE components.
flashcards.back: Speech: articulation, phonology, fluency, voice. Language: semantics, morphology, syntax, pragmatics.
flashcards.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: What is a morpheme?
flashcards.back: The smallest unit of meaning in a language.
flashcards.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: What are suprasegmentals?
flashcards.back: Features layered over speech sounds that convey meaning: pitch, rate, and stress.
flashcards.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: What is echolalia?
flashcards.back: Imitation of words/phrases/sentences without understanding their meaning.
flashcards.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: List the five levels of the speech chain in order.
flashcards.back: Linguistic → physiological → acoustic → physiological → linguistic ('brain to brain').
flashcards.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: Who compiled the design features that distinguish human communication?
flashcards.back: Charles Hockett (the Characteristics of Human Communication).
flashcards.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

flashcards.front: Name Skinner's five verbal operants.
flashcards.back: Echoic (imitation), Tact (labeling), Mand (requesting), Intraverbal (social talk), Autoclitic (combining words from experience).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: Which verbal operant is requesting?
flashcards.back: The mand.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: Which verbal operant is labeling?
flashcards.back: The tact.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: What is a discriminative stimulus?
flashcards.back: A prompt or cue that occurs before a target behavior signaling reinforcement is available (e.g., pointing to the letter L to cue /l/).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: Shaping vs. chaining?
flashcards.back: Shaping = reinforcing successive approximations toward a target. Chaining = teaching the sequence of steps that make up a behavior.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: In behaviorism, does 'negative' mean bad?
flashcards.back: No — 'negative' means something is REMOVED from the environment (reinforcement or punishment).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: Give the four operant-conditioning quadrants.
flashcards.back: Positive reinforcement (add good → ↑), negative reinforcement (remove bad → ↑), positive punishment (add bad → ↓), negative punishment (remove good → ↓).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: Who is associated with classical conditioning, and what is it?
flashcards.back: Ivan Pavlov — a neutral (conditioned) stimulus comes to trigger a response through association (e.g., learning the meaning of 'sit').
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: What are 'virtuous errors' and what do they show?
flashcards.back: Rule over-generalizations like 'drinked' for 'drank'; they show the child is actively applying rules, not just imitating — an argument against pure behaviorism.
flashcards.source: Theories of Language Acquisition (handout)

flashcards.front: What is the critical period, and which case illustrates it?
flashcards.back: A window (~to age 7) after which a first language can't be fully acquired; illustrated by Genie, isolated until age 13, who never gained full grammar.
flashcards.source: Theories of Language Acquisition (handout)

flashcards.front: How do creoles support the innateness theory?
flashcards.back: Children of pidgin-speakers spontaneously turn a restricted pidgin into a full, rule-governed creole — evidence of the LAD at work (Bickerton).
flashcards.source: Theories of Language Acquisition (handout)

flashcards.front: How did Slobin modify Chomsky's LAD?
flashcards.back: He recast the LAD as a process mechanism for working out language rules, rather than a store of fixed linguistic categories.
flashcards.source: Theories of Language Acquisition (handout)

flashcards.front: In Fillmore's semantic view, what are modality and proposition?
flashcards.back: Modality = verb tense, negation, interrogation. Proposition = the noun–verb relationship (the core of meaning).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: What is a 'case' in Fillmore's theory?
flashcards.back: A semantic role a noun phrase can fill; the verb determines which cases its nouns take (agentive, dative, experiencer, factitive, instrumental, locative, objective).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: Piaget's cognitive view: what must precede using words like 'bigger'?
flashcards.back: Seriation — the ability to order objects by size — must develop before the comparative language for it.
flashcards.source: Theories of Language Acquisition (handout)

flashcards.front: What is object permanence and why does it matter for language?
flashcards.back: Knowing objects exist when out of sight (~18 mo); it's linked to the jump in object-labeling vocabulary.
flashcards.source: Theories of Language Acquisition (handout)

flashcards.front: What is Bruner's LASS?
flashcards.back: The Language Acquisition Support System — the social support structure (caregiver interaction, scaffolding) that supports acquisition; the social counterpart to Chomsky's LAD.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: What is scaffolding?
flashcards.back: Caregiver support adjusted to the child's level that increases in complexity as the child's ability grows.
flashcards.source: Theories of Language Acquisition (handout)

flashcards.front: What is expansion (in parentese)?
flashcards.back: An adult repeats a child's utterance while adding words, reordering, or adding structure to model more complex language.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: Who launched the 'pragmatics revolution' and what is its core idea?
flashcards.back: Austin and Searle — language is produced with an outcome in mind, analyzed through speech acts.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: Whose research showed pre-verbal turn-taking, and how?
flashcards.back: Colwyn Trevarthen — turn-taking develops through games and non-verbal exchange before words appear.
flashcards.source: Theories of Language Acquisition (handout)

flashcards.front: Why does behaviorism fall on the 'nurture' side?
flashcards.back: It holds that language is learned through imitation, reinforcement, and successive approximations — a product of the environment.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: Which SLP populations often benefit from Skinner-based (behaviorist) intervention?
flashcards.back: Children with autism and other developmental disabilities (ABA-style approaches).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

flashcards.front: The McNeill 'nobody don't like me' exchange illustrates what?
flashcards.back: That children often can't simply repeat an adult structure they haven't yet acquired — evidence against imitation-only accounts.
flashcards.source: Theories of Language Acquisition (handout)

flashcards.front: What is a schema in Piaget's theory?
flashcards.back: The mental 'file-folder' system that organizes knowledge for processing, storing, and retrieving information.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: Assimilation vs. accommodation?
flashcards.back: Assimilation = fitting new info into an EXISTING schema. Accommodation = making a NEW schema (or reorganizing) when it doesn't fit.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: What is equilibrium?
flashcards.back: Keeping assimilation and accommodation in balance as schemata are built and reorganized.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: Use the pantry analogy for assimilation vs. accommodation.
flashcards.back: Filing chips under existing 'dry goods' = assimilation; creating a new 'snacks' shelf when you have too many = accommodation; the ongoing rebalancing = equilibrium.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: List Piaget's four stages with age ranges.
flashcards.back: Sensorimotor (birth-2), Preoperational (2-7), Concrete operations (7-11), Formal operations (11-15).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: Why is sensorimotor development important for language?
flashcards.back: It is prerequisite to language — you need many sensorimotor skills before you're ready to develop language.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: Name the six key sensorimotor skills.
flashcards.back: Object permanence, causality, means/ends, imitation, play, communication.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: What is object permanence?
flashcards.back: Understanding that things still exist even when they're outside your five senses (builds a cognitive representation of them).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: What are means/ends?
flashcards.back: Using cause and effect to figure out the actions (means) that accomplish a goal (end) — through actions or words.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: What is symbolic play and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: Using one object to represent another; crucial for language because words are symbolic representations of things/concepts.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: What is deferred imitation and when does it appear?
flashcards.back: Imitating something later from memory (no model present); it appears in sensorimotor substage 6.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: What is distancing?
flashcards.back: The developing ability to perceive things from greater and greater distances, leading toward naming and representation.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: When do true first words appear vs. babbling?
flashcards.back: Babbling (CV sounds) begins ~substage 3; 'mama'/'dada' aren't true words until produced consistently, intentionally, and meaningfully.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: Sensorimotor substage 1 (birth-1 mo): hallmark?
flashcards.back: World revolves around the infant; no means-end or object concept; highly reflexive, automatic actions.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: Sensorimotor substage 4 (8-12 mo): hallmark?
flashcards.back: Object permanence begins (searches for hidden objects); causality with intent; imitates unfamiliar/unseen behaviors; babbling may become first words.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: Sensorimotor substage 6 (18-24 mo): hallmark?
flashcards.back: Representational thinking (solve problems mentally); object permanence fully developed; deferred imitation; more complex pretend play.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: How did research revise Piaget's sensorimotor claims?
flashcards.back: Babies move through the substages and show some skills EARLIER than he thought, and knowledge includes perceptual (seen/heard) experiences, not only felt ones.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: Preoperational thought (2-7): key features?
flashcards.back: Rapid language growth; learning via hands-on visual/motor tasks; egocentric; problem solving focuses on one element at a time.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: Formal operations (11-15): key ability?
flashcards.back: Abstract thinking — combining prior knowledge with new information and planning for tasks.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

flashcards.front: What three things make up socioeconomic status (SES)?
flashcards.back: Family income, parental education, and parental occupation.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: What is the 'word gap'?
flashcards.back: The ~30-million-word difference in language exposure by age 3 between children from the wealthiest vs. poorest families.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: What is contingent responding?
flashcards.back: A back-and-forth where the infant initiates, the caregiver responds, and the infant responds back.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: What is joint reference (joint attention) and when does it begin?
flashcards.back: Sharing the same focus of attention with a caregiver (~2 months); it requires shared eye contact and gaze/point following and sets the stage for language.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: Expansion vs. extension?
flashcards.back: Expansion = repeat the child's utterance with fuller GRAMMAR ('shoe' → 'put shoes on'). Extension = add SEMANTIC info ('shoe' → 'let's put your red shoes on').
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: Fast mapping vs. slow (extended) mapping?
flashcards.back: Fast mapping = learning a word after even one exposure (not yet long-term). Slow/extended mapping = building fuller meaning through repeated, varied exposure.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: What is a phonological representation?
flashcards.back: The stored sound pattern for a word that lets us retrieve its associated thing/concept when we hear it.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: Name the three hypotheses of word-meaning learning.
flashcards.back: Semantic feature hypothesis, functional core hypothesis, and prototype hypothesis.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: Name Bates' three stages of communicative development.
flashcards.back: Perlocutionary (birth-8 mo, reflexive), illocutionary (8-12 mo, intentional gestures/vocalizations), locutionary (first true words).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: Trace the progression of vocalizations from birth to ~12 months.
flashcards.back: Reflexive cries → cooing (~2 mo) → transitional babbling (~5 mo) → reduplicated babbling (~6-7 mo) → variegated babbling & jargon (~9 mo) → first words (~12 mo).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: Reduplicated vs. variegated babbling?
flashcards.back: Reduplicated = repeated identical CV syllables ('baba'). Variegated = combinations of DIFFERING sounds, more word-like (CVC).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: What is jargon?
flashcards.back: Babbling with adult-like intonation, stress, and rhythm.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: What are vocables?
flashcards.back: Self-invented sound combinations a child uses consistently and meaningfully — early intentional communication.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: Deictic vs. representational gestures?
flashcards.back: Deictic = pointing something out (reaching, pointing, waving, giving). Representational = pretend-play or social gestures.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: Protodeclaratives vs. protoimperatives (Bates)?
flashcards.back: Protodeclaratives = point to share/joint attention. Protoimperatives = point to demand or control others.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: Why is lack of pointing around 12 months a concern?
flashcards.back: It's often considered a red flag for autism.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: Overextension vs. underextension?
flashcards.back: Overextension = one word for too many things ('da' for dog AND cat). Underextension = a word for only one specific thing ('bee' only for one blanket).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: Halliday vs. Dore — what did each categorize?
flashcards.back: Halliday: 7 communicative FUNCTIONS. Dore: primitive speech acts (PSA) of the one-word stage (labeling, requesting, etc.).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: What is mean length of utterance (MLU)?
flashcards.back: The average number of morphemes per utterance — a measure of syntactic development (Brown).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: Early vs. Late Stage 1 (Brown)?
flashcards.back: Early Stage 1 ≈ MLU 1.0-1.5 (mostly single words); Late Stage 1 ≈ MLU 1.5-2.0 (two-word combinations emerge).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: What is presupposition?
flashcards.back: Assuming/interpreting what a listener already knows so as not to overshare; begins ~18 months.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: Which side of the nature/nurture debate do the SES/word-gap findings support?
flashcards.back: Nurture — more caregiver talk predicts higher vocabulary, IQ, and later language skills.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: List several factors that influence language development.
flashcards.back: Race/ethnicity; social class, education & occupation; region; gender; situation/context; peer group; first-language community/culture.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: What is infant-directed singing?
flashcards.back: Caregiver singing (lullabies) that soothes and builds attachment by matching a calming emotional state.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

flashcards.front: How did Vygotsky's view of development differ from Piaget's?
flashcards.back: Both combined nature and nurture, but Piaget saw a universal progression of stages, while Vygotsky saw development as a UNIQUE experience shaped by each child's social, cultural, and environmental interactions.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

flashcards.front: What is private speech, and how does it change with age?
flashcards.back: Self-talk used to direct action, learning, planning, and problem-solving; it starts out loud, becomes a whisper, and is eventually internalized as inner thought (Vygotsky).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

flashcards.front: What is the zone of proximal development (ZPD)?
flashcards.back: The range of skills a child can do WITH assistance but not yet independently; we support the next level rather than demanding skills out of range. (Review — introduced earlier.)
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

flashcards.front: What is scaffolding and what's the goal?
flashcards.back: Support given to help someone accomplish a task within their ZPD, faded as they move toward doing it independently. (Review — introduced earlier.)
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

flashcards.front: What is shape bias?
flashcards.back: Relating and extending a new word to other objects based on similar shape, using perception and prior knowledge.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

flashcards.front: What are executive functions, and when are they fully developed?
flashcards.back: Control processes for maintaining attention, inhibiting irrelevant associations, and using working memory; not fully developed until the mid-20s.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

flashcards.front: What is controlled attention?
flashcards.back: Maintaining attention on a task while ignoring internal and external distractions.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

flashcards.front: Why is working memory important?
flashcards.back: It lets us take in, hold, process, and retrieve task-relevant information and is one of the biggest predictors of learning ability.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

flashcards.front: Name the two working-memory storage systems and what each does.
flashcards.back: Phonological loop = temporary storage of verbal information; visual-spatial sketchpad = creating and adjusting mental images.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

flashcards.front: What is theory of mind?
flashcards.back: Understanding that others have their own perspectives, beliefs, intentions, thoughts, and emotions, which may differ from one's own; develops alongside language.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

flashcards.front: Explain the crayon-box theory-of-mind task.
flashcards.back: Jason hides candy in a crayon box; asked what Susie will think is inside, a child WITH theory of mind says 'crayons' (Susie didn't see the candy), while a child WITHOUT says 'candy.'
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

flashcards.front: How do visual-tactile and auditory perception support early language?
flashcards.back: Visual/tactile input draws attention and supports parent-child bonding (babies are prewired for faces); auditory perception lets infants discriminate speech, recognize mother's voice, and attend to the human voice — evidence of innate speech processing.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

flashcards.front: Free vs. bound morpheme?
flashcards.back: Free = can stand alone as a word ('dog'). Bound = must attach to a word (prefixes, suffixes, endings like -ed/-s).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: Derivational vs. inflectional morphemes?
flashcards.back: Derivational = prefixes/suffixes that make a new word or change its category ('re-', '-er'). Inflectional = grammatical-marker suffixes (plural, possession, tense) that DON'T change category ('-ed', '-s').
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: What is a grammatical morpheme, and how many did Brown identify?
flashcards.back: A morpheme that signals grammatical relationships; Brown identified 14 acquired in a fairly predictable order.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: When is a grammatical morpheme considered mastered?
flashcards.back: When used correctly in ~90% of its obligatory contexts (places Standard English requires it).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: Name the first few of Brown's 14 morphemes in order.
flashcards.back: 1) present progressive -ing, 2) preposition 'in', 3) preposition 'on', 4) regular plural -s, 5) irregular past tense, 6) possessive 's, 7) uncontractible copula…
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: What are two-word semantic relations, and which stage?
flashcards.back: The meaning a child shows by combining two words (agent+action, action+object, possessor+possession, etc.); typical of Brown's Stage I.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: Give the MLU ranges for Early vs. Late Stage 1.
flashcards.back: Early Stage 1 ≈ MLU 1.0-1.5 (one-word utterances); Late Stage 1 ≈ MLU 1.5-2.0 (two-word combinations emerge). [Review from Module 6]
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: Count the morphemes: 'The dog runs fast.'
flashcards.back: 5 morphemes — the / dog / run / -s / fast (4 words, but 'runs' = run + -s).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: How do you calculate MLU?
flashcards.back: Count the total morphemes across the sample and divide by the number of utterances.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: What is an utterance for MLU purposes?
flashcards.back: Typically one thought, often signaled by a pause.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: Name the three new speech functions at the two-word stage.
flashcards.back: Mathetic (for learning), informative (telling what you know), and pragmatic (getting something done).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: Does comprehension or production come first? Evidence?
flashcards.back: Comprehension precedes production — e.g., Benedict found ~13-month-olds could understand ~50 words but produce only ~10.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: Reliability vs. validity in language sampling?
flashcards.back: Reliability = the sample truly represents the child's typical abilities. Validity = the sample measures what it's meant to measure.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: What is glossing?
flashcards.back: Repeating aloud what a child said while recording, so it can be understood later during transcription.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: In MLU counting, what counts as ONE morpheme even though it may look like more?
flashcards.back: Diminutives (doggie), compound words (hotdog), catenatives (gonna/wanna), irregular past tense (went) and irregular plurals (mice), reduplications (choo-choo), proper names (Big Bird).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: In MLU counting, what counts as MORE than one morpheme?
flashcards.back: Contractions (she's, can't — except let's/don't/won't), inflections (plural/possessive/past/3rd-person/-ing), and comparative/superlative forms.
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: What is the type-token ratio (TTR)?
flashcards.back: Different words ÷ total words — a measure of vocabulary diversity (~0.5 for young children).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

flashcards.front: What are good vs. poor elicitation strategies for a sample?
flashcards.back: Good: open-ended prompts ('Tell me about…', 'I wonder what…'), follow the child's lead/interests. Poor: yes/no questions and the 'name game' (just labeling).
flashcards.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

questions.text: Explain how Boyle's Law drives one full cycle of respiration (inhalation and exhalation).
questions.answer: As the diaphragm contracts and flattens (and the ribs swing up and out), the volume of the thorax increases, which decreases pressure; to equalize with outside pressure, air is forced into the lungs (inhalation). When the muscles relax, the diaphragm returns to its dome shape and the ribs lower, decreasing thoracic volume and increasing pressure, so air flows out of the lungs (exhalation). One inhalation + exhalation completes a cycle.
questions.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

questions.text: List the 5 steps of the phonation process.
questions.answer: 1) The adductors bring the vocal folds together, restricting airflow. 2) Exhaled air pressure builds beneath the adducted folds. 3) Pressure blows the folds apart, releasing a puff of air into the trachea. 4) After release, the pressure drops. 5) The pressure drop plus fold elasticity snaps the folds back together, and the cycle repeats.
questions.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

questions.text: Describe the path of sound through the ear from the pinna to the auditory nerve.
questions.answer: The pinna directs sound into the external auditory meatus (ear canal) to the tympanic membrane (eardrum), which vibrates. That vibration passes along the ossicles — malleus, then incus, then stapes. The stapes footplate moves the oval window, setting the cochlear fluids in motion; this moves the tectorial membrane, which triggers the inner hair cells (arranged by frequency). The auditory nerve then carries the signal to the brain.
questions.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

questions.text: Compare and contrast the nativist and behaviorist perspectives on language acquisition.
questions.answer: Nativism (Chomsky) argues for NATURE: language is innate and biologically based, driven by an innate LAD, acquired early and universally with the environment acting only as a trigger. Behaviorism (Skinner) argues for NURTURE: language is a learned behavior, with the environment as the critical factor, shaped through operant conditioning (reinforcement and punishment); the child is treated like an 'empty vessel' filled by experience. Nativism stresses innate competence and linguistic universals; behaviorism stresses environmental modeling and learning.

questions.text: Describe the speech chain and the levels a message passes through.
questions.answer: The speech chain describes the connection between a speaker and a listener. The speaker forms a thought and selects/orders words (linguistic level), the brain sends motor commands to the speech systems which produce speech (physiological level), sound waves travel to the listener (acoustic level), the listener's hearing mechanism captures the sound (physiological level), and the listener's brain interprets the message (linguistic level) — brain to brain.
