notes.title: Language Sampling & Calculating MLU
notes.body:
A language sample captures all the language a child produces during interaction (usually audio/video recorded, then transcribed word-for-word) to analyze syntax, grammar, semantics, and pragmatics.

QUALITY
- Reliability: the sample truly represents the child's typical abilities.
- Validity: it measures what it's meant to measure (not just singing or yes/no answers).

ELICITING A GOOD SAMPLE
- Let the child lead; use open-ended prompts ("Tell me about…", "How did…", "I wonder what…"); use "why" sparingly under age 4.
- Avoid yes/no questions and the "name game" (just labeling).
- Activities by age: toddlers (toys, books, snack), preschoolers (pretend play, books), school-age (conversation, narratives).
- Glossing: repeat the child's words aloud while recording to aid later transcription.

CALCULATING MLU
- Segment into utterances (one thought, signaled by a pause). Aim for 75-100 usable utterances.
- MLU = total morphemes ÷ number of utterances.
- Count as ONE: diminutives (doggie), compounds (hotdog), catenatives (gonna), irregular past (went) & irregular plurals (mice), reduplications (choo-choo), proper names (Big Bird), plurals with no singular (pants) and plural pronouns (us).
- Count as MORE THAN ONE: contractions (she's, can't — except let's/don't/won't), inflections (plural/possessive/past/3rd-person/-ing), comparatives/superlatives.
- Do NOT count: fillers (um), unintelligible/interrupted utterances, immediate imitations, elliptical one-word answers, false starts/reformulations, rhymes/songs/counting, noises.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Reliability (representative) vs. validity (measures the right thing).
- MLU = total morphemes ÷ utterances; aim for 75-100 utterances.
- Know the count-as-one vs. count-as-more-than-one rules.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

notes.title: Semantic, Pragmatic & Comprehension Levels
notes.body:
SEMANTIC LEVEL — meaning created by the words used. For short utterances, semantic analysis is informative via two/three-word semantic relations, Halliday's communicative functions, or Dore's primitive speech acts. Vocabulary diversity can be measured with the type-token ratio (different words ÷ total words; ~0.5 in young children).

PRAGMATIC LEVEL — social use of language (greetings, requesting, asking questions, appropriateness of responses, maintaining topics). At the two-word stage, children expand communicative intentions and develop new functions:
- Mathetic function: using language for learning.
- Informative function: telling someone something they don't know.
- Pragmatic function: using language to get something done.

COMPREHENSION BEFORE PRODUCTION — receptive language is thought to develop before expressive. Babies respond to questions/emotions before understanding words, and comprehend words before producing them (Benedict: ~13 months, ~50 words understood vs. ~10 produced). Children first comprehend words from daily routines and build mental representations from exposure.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Mathetic (learn) / informative (tell) / pragmatic (get things done).
- Type-token ratio ≈ 0.5 for young children.
- Comprehension precedes production (Benedict ~50 understood vs. ~10 produced at 13 mo).
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

notes.title: Two-Word Semantic Relations (Brown's Stage I)
notes.body:
When toddlers combine two words, the meaning is shown by the RELATIONSHIP between the words (Bloom's semantic-syntactic relations). Context decides the relation — "Mommy sock" could be possessor+possession (Mommy's sock) OR agent+object (Mommy putting a sock on), so always note what was happening.

Brown's eight most common relations:
- Agent + Action — "Mommy eat"
- Action + Object — "Kick ball"
- Agent + Object (verb omitted) — "Daddy ball"
- Action + Locative — "Go outside"
- Entity + Locative — "Cup table"
- Possessor + Possession — "My truck"
- Entity + Attribute — "Big dog"
- Demonstrative + Entity — "That car"

Other common relations: Recurrence ("More juice"), Nonexistence/Disappearance ("Allgone cookie"), Rejection ("No bath"), Denial ("No doggy" when a cat is called a dog), Notice/Greeting ("Hi Mommy").

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Meaning comes from the relation, not grammar.
- Context disambiguates (e.g., "Mommy sock").
- Nonexistence (gone) vs. Rejection (refused) vs. Denial (untrue).
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

notes.title: Brown's 14 Grammatical Morphemes
notes.body:
Brown (1973) identified 14 grammatical morphemes acquired in a fairly predictable order. A morpheme is counted as mastered when used correctly in ~90% of obligatory contexts (places Standard English requires it).

Typical order of acquisition:
1. Present progressive -ing (no helping verb) — "Mommy driving"
2. Preposition "in" — "Ball in box"
3. Preposition "on" — "Cup on table"
4. Regular plural -s — "cats, dogs, horses"
5. Irregular past tense — "fell, broke, went"
6. Possessive 's — "Daddy's car"
7. Uncontractible copula (be as main verb, can't shorten) — "Who's sick?" → "He is."
8. Articles a, the — "a cookie", "the dog"
9. Regular past tense -ed — "jumped, played, painted"
10. Regular third person singular -s — "She runs"
11. Irregular third person singular — "She has", "He does"
12. Uncontractible auxiliary (be as helper, can't shorten) — "Who's running?" → "He is."
13. Contractible copula — "She's happy"
14. Contractible auxiliary — "He's running"

Tricky distinctions:
- Copula vs. auxiliary: is "be" helping an -ing verb? Yes = auxiliary, No = copula ("She is tall" copula vs. "She is eating" auxiliary).
- Contractible vs. uncontractible: could it be shortened in that exact spot? ("He is nice" contractible vs. "Yes, he is" uncontractible).
- Plural vs. possessive vs. 3rd-person -s: noun meaning "more than one" vs. ownership vs. a he/she/it verb ("cats" / "cat's toy" / "she eats").

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- -ing is first; the contractible copula/auxiliary are last.
- 90% in obligatory contexts = mastered.
- Know copula vs. auxiliary and contractible vs. uncontractible.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

notes.title: Brown's Stages & the Four Levels of Analysis
notes.body:
As children move past single words, they combine words and add morphemes, increasing complexity. MLU (average meaningful units per utterance) is tracked against Brown's Stages of Syntactic Development (MLU ranges ↔ stages ↔ ages).

- Early Stage 1 (MLU 1.0-1.5; ~12-22 mo): mostly one-word, one-morpheme utterances; a mix of jargon and single words; "strings" of single words that aren't true combinations. [review from Mod 6]
- Late Stage 1 (MLU 1.5-2.0; ~22-26 mo): two-word combinations emerge (18-24 mo), with some 3-4 word combos; little morphology yet. [review]

FOUR LEVELS we analyze language on:
1. Syntax — sentence structure.
2. Grammar / morphology — the rules for constructing words and sentences.
3. Semantics — meaning.
4. Pragmatics — social use.
(Syntax and grammar overlap; treat syntax as structure and grammar/morphology as the rules.)

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- MLU = total morphemes ÷ total utterances; tracked on Brown's stages.
- Early Stage 1 = one-word; Late Stage 1 = two-word combinations.
- Four levels: syntax, grammar, semantics, pragmatics.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

notes.title: Morphemes & Word Structure
notes.body:
Morphemes are the smallest grammatical units that carry meaning. They can be whole words, word parts (prefixes, suffixes, roots), or grammatical endings.

- Free morpheme: stands alone as a word (e.g., "dog", "run").
- Bound morpheme: must attach to a word (prefixes, suffixes, grammatical endings like -ed, -s).
- Derivational morphemes = prefixes and suffixes that create a new word or change its category:
  • Prefix: added to the beginning ("re-" in "replay").
  • Suffix: added to the end, can change category ("-er" in "teacher").
- Inflectional morphemes: suffixes that act as grammatical markers (plurality, possession, verb tense) WITHOUT changing category (e.g., "-ed" past tense, "-s" plural/possessive).
- Root word: the base carrying core meaning.

Counting example (words vs. morphemes):
- "The dog runs fast" = 4 words, but 5 morphemes (the / dog / run / -s / fast).
- "mom's running fast" = 3 words, but 5 morphemes (mom / -s / run / -ing / fast).

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Free (alone) vs. bound (attached).
- Derivational = new word/category; inflectional = grammatical marker, same category.
- Be able to split words into morphemes for MLU.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 7: Emerging Syntax & Language Samples (Ch. 4-5)

notes.title: Theory of Mind
notes.body:
Theory of mind is our grasp of the inner workings of perspectives, beliefs, intentions, thoughts, and emotions — our own and others'. It develops alongside language.

EXAMPLES
- Toddlers coming to understand that caregivers are independent of them.
- Recognizing others' emotions.
- Understanding that others may hold a different view/perspective.

FALSE-BELIEF CHECK (crayon-box task)
Jason puts candy into a crayon box. Asked what his friend Susie will think is inside:
- WITH theory of mind → "crayons" (Susie never saw the candy).
- WITHOUT theory of mind → "candy" (the child knows the candy is there and can't separate their own knowledge from Susie's).

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Theory of mind = understanding others have separate minds/perspectives.
- The crayon-box false-belief task: correct answer is "crayons."
- Develops alongside language.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

notes.title: Executive Functions, Attention & Memory
notes.body:
EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS
Control processes in the brain that let us maintain attention, inhibit irrelevant associations, and use working memory. They are NOT fully developed until the mid-20s — which helps explain impulsive, irrational decisions in children, teens, and young adults.

ATTENTION & MEMORY (vital for language and learning — you can't have one without the other)
- Controlled attention: maintaining attention while ignoring internal/external distractions.
- Working memory: taking in, processing, holding, and retrieving task-relevant information; one of the biggest predictors of learning ability. Two storage systems:
  1. Phonological loop — temporary storage of verbal messages/information (for long-term memory or speech).
  2. Visual-spatial sketchpad — creating and adjusting mental images.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Executive functions = attention + inhibition + working memory; mature in the mid-20s.
- Working memory = top predictor of learning ability.
- Two systems: phonological loop (verbal) vs. visual-spatial sketchpad (images).
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

notes.title: Development of Perception
notes.body:
Perception is how a person selects, organizes, integrates, and interprets sensory stimuli. Perception and cognition develop together as the senses mature.

- Visual-tactile perception: early on, visual/tactile input draws attention (helping the child attend to the auditory stimuli crucial for language) and supports parent-child bonding. Infants are prewired to be interested in the features/shapes of human faces, aiding the early bond; joint attention (shared child-caregiver attention) is necessary for language development. [joint attention — review]
- Auditory perception: infants can discriminate the sounds of all languages at birth (seen in head turns toward sound); early on they can detect when sounds begin/end, recognize the mother's voice, and tell speech from non-speech. This interest in the human voice is evidence of an innate ability to receive and process speech. With exposure, discrimination narrows to the sounds of the child's own language/culture.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Perception = select, organize, integrate, interpret sensory input.
- Visual/tactile first draws attention and bonds; auditory enables speech discrimination.
- Innate broad sound discrimination narrows to the native language with exposure.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

notes.title: Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory (vs. Piaget)
notes.body:
Like Piaget, Lev Vygotsky's theory combines NATURE and NURTURE: children are born with abilities that are shaped by environmental and cultural exploration. But the views differ:
- Piaget: children progress through a UNIVERSAL sequence of stages.
- Vygotsky: development is a UNIQUE experience for each child, driven by social, environmental, and cultural interaction.

KEY IDEAS
- Private speech: self-talk used to direct actions, learning, planning, and problem-solving. Starts out loud → becomes a whisper → internalized as inner thought (the mental chatter we use all day).
- Zone of proximal development (ZPD) [review]: the range of skills a child can do WITH assistance but not yet independently. Don't demand out-of-range skills — support the next level.
- Scaffolding [review]: supports given to help accomplish a task within the ZPD, FADED as the child nears independence.
- Shape bias: children relate and extend new words to other objects based on similar shape, using perception and prior knowledge.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Piaget = universal stages; Vygotsky = unique, social/cultural.
- Private speech progression: aloud → whisper → internal.
- ZPD = "with help but not alone"; scaffolding = support that fades.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 5: Cognitive Development II - Vygotsky (Ch. 3, pp. 89-108)

notes.title: Gestures, First Words & Communicative Functions
notes.body:
GESTURES
- Deictic gestures: point something out (reaching, pointing, waving, giving).
- Representational gestures: more sophisticated (pretend play; social gestures).
- Bates' two types of pointing:
  • Protodeclaratives — point to share/establish joint attention.
  • Protoimperatives — point to make demands or control others.
- RED FLAG: lack of pointing ~12 months can indicate autism risk.

FIRST WORDS (~12 months)
- Limited sound inventory; words are familiar/high-interest; simplified (CV like "ba" for bottle, or duplicated CVCV like "mama").
- Overextension: one word for too many referents ("da" for dog and cat).
- Underextension: a word for only one specific referent ("bee" only for one blanket).

COMMUNICATIVE PURPOSE
- Halliday's communicative functions: 7 categories of WHY a child communicates.
- Dore's primitive speech acts (PSA) of the one-word stage: labeling, answering, requesting an action, requesting an answer, calling, greeting, protesting, repeating/imitating, practicing.

SYNTAX MEASURE & CONVERSATION
- Mean length of utterance (MLU): average morphemes per utterance (Brown). Early Stage 1 ≈ MLU 1.0-1.5 (single words); Late Stage 1 ≈ MLU 1.5-2.0 (two-word combos emerge).
- Presupposition: assuming what a listener already knows so as not to overshare; begins ~18 months.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Deictic (point out) vs. representational (pretend/social); protodeclarative (share) vs. protoimperative (demand).
- Overextension (too broad) vs. underextension (too narrow).
- Halliday = functions; Dore = primitive speech acts; MLU = morphemes per utterance.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

notes.title: Prelinguistic Vocal Development (Bates' Stages)
notes.body:
BATES' STAGES OF COMMUNICATIVE DEVELOPMENT
- Perlocutionary stage (birth-8 mo): baby responds reflexively; caregivers interpret intent.
- Illocutionary stage (8-12 mo): intentional vocalizations + gestures express messages (before true words); pointing and imitation advance.
- Locutionary stage: first true words / intentional communication.

VOCALIZATION PROGRESSION
- Reflexive cries (birth) → differentiated cries (hunger, pain, anger ~1 mo; discomfort/call/request ~2 mo).
- Cooing (~2 mo): vowel-like pleasure sounds; start of back-and-forth.
- Transitional babbling (~5 mo): cooing → single-syllable V/C sounds.
- Reduplicated babbling (~6-7 mo): repeated identical CV syllables; front sounds (m, p, b, t, d, n).
- Echolalia (8-12 mo): imitates sounds/syllables/words without true meaning.
- Variegated babbling (~9 mo): differing-sound CV combinations, word-like (CVC).
- Jargon: adult-like intonation/stress/rhythm; mixes with early true words.
- Vocables: consistent self-invented sound combos used meaningfully — early intentional communication.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Order: cries → cooing → transitional → reduplicated → variegated/jargon → words.
- Reduplicated = same syllable repeated; variegated = different sounds combined.
- Bates: perlocutionary (reflexive) → illocutionary (intentional gestures) → locutionary (words).
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

notes.title: Word Learning
notes.body:
Infants need good hearing to discriminate speech sounds, words, and intonation; keep words in memory; and learn speech patterns.

- Phonotactic patterns: the rules for how sounds combine in a language.
- Phonological representations: stored sound patterns for words (root "phon" = sound); hearing a word retrieves its associated thing/concept.
- Word-learning sequence: hear the word (auditory cue) → activate the sound pattern (phonological representation) → connect to the thing/concept (semantic level) → comprehension.
- Fast mapping: learn a word after even ONE exposure (before age 1); not yet held long-term.
- Slow/extended mapping: build deeper meaning through repeated, varied exposure.
- Shift over time: early word learning leans on phonological representations; by ~2 years (a language spurt) children rely more on the SEMANTIC level.

THREE HYPOTHESES OF WORD MEANING
- Semantic feature hypothesis: meaning via distinguishing (usually perceptual) features.
- Functional core hypothesis: meaning via what animate/inanimate things DO.
- Prototype hypothesis: form a model/prototype of features + function; fit new words to it.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Fast mapping (one exposure, not retained) vs. slow/extended mapping (repeated, deeper).
- Sequence: auditory cue → phonological representation → semantic connection.
- Know the 3 hypotheses by their core idea.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

notes.title: Parent-Child & Child-Directed Interactions
notes.body:
Preparation begins in the womb (exposure to the mother's voice, rhythms, taste, smell). Early supports:
- Infant-directed singing: lullabies soothe and build attachment by matching a calming emotional state.
- Rhymes & stories: teach turn-taking structure, build word awareness, and help children predict how stories go.

CHILD-DIRECTED INTERACTIONS
- Contingent responding: infant initiates → caregiver responds → infant responds back.
- Joint reference (joint attention): sharing the same focus with a caregiver (~2 months); needs shared eye contact and gaze/point following; sets the stage for language.
- Motherese/parentese (review): higher pitch, exaggerated intonation, shorter/simpler phrases, slower rate, more repetition, exaggerated facial expressions.
- Expansion (review): repeat the child's utterance with fuller grammar ("shoe" → "put shoes on").
- Extension: add semantic information ("shoe" → "let's put your red shoes on").

FACILITATING A STRONG LANGUAGE ENVIRONMENT
Start from birth, be responsive, follow the child's lead/interests, use expansions and extensions, share picture books and simple stories.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Contingent responding = the initiate-respond-respond loop.
- Joint reference ~2 months = foundation for language.
- Expansion = grammar; Extension = meaning.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

notes.title: SES, Influencing Factors & the Word Gap
notes.body:
Infants are born able to discriminate the speech sounds of ALL languages; experience shapes speech/language to their culture and environment.

SEVEN FACTORS THAT INFLUENCE LANGUAGE DEVELOPMENT
1. Race and ethnicity
2. Social class, education, and occupation
3. Region
4. Gender
5. Situation or context
6. Peer group association or identification
7. First-language community or culture

SOCIOECONOMIC STATUS (SES)
- "A person's SES includes family income, parental education, and occupation of the parents."
- Impacts health (prenatal/health care, nourishment, environmental exposure), safety (living conditions, access to drugs/weapons), and education (parent education level, absences, limited language/literacy exposure).

THE WORD GAP
- Language tracked by SES: low-income ~616 words/hr, working-class ~1,251/hr, professional ~2,153/hr.
- Projected ~30-million-word gap by age 3 between wealthiest and poorest families.
- More caregiver talk → higher vocabulary and IQ at 3, stronger language at 9-10. It's not only the NUMBER of words but exposure across many CONTEXTS (e.g., "water" for a drink, watering a plant, filling the tub).

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- SES = income + parental education + parental occupation.
- Word gap ≈ 30 million words by age 3; supports the NURTURE side.
- Language-rich = same word modeled across varied contexts.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 6: Communication Development Birth-2 (Ch. 4)

notes.title: Theories at a Glance — Nature / Nurture Placement
notes.body:
Use this to place each theory and theorist on the nature–nurture continuum.

- NATIVIST — NATURE. Chomsky: LAD, universal rules, transformational generative grammar (deep → transformations → surface).
- BEHAVIORIST — NURTURE. Skinner: operant conditioning, verbal operants, imitation/reinforcement; Pavlov: classical conditioning.
- INTERACTIONIST — NATURE + NURTURE. Combination of genetics and environment. Views:
  • Semantic — Fillmore (meaning via word relationships).
  • Cognitive — Piaget (language follows cognitive development).
  • Social Interactionist — Bruner (LASS, scaffolding, caregiver interaction).
  • Pragmatics Revolution — Austin & Searle (speech acts; language to achieve outcomes).

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Nativist = nature; Behaviorist = nurture; Interactionist = both.
- Match each theorist to their view and their nature/nurture side.
- These theories are complementary — each explains part of the process, not competing replacements.
notes.source: Theories of Language Development (S. Herrera) — Module 3 deck

notes.title: Interactionism — Pragmatics Revolution (Austin & Searle)
notes.body:
PRAGMATICS REVOLUTION — Austin & Searle
Language is produced with an OUTCOME in mind. The purpose of speech is analyzed as three speech acts:
1. Locutionary act — the actual message/words that are heard.
2. Illocutionary act — the motive or purpose behind the message (indirect speech). E.g., a child seeing cookies says "I love cookies" — the motive is to get a cookie.
3. Perlocutionary act — the effect the message has on the listener; a breakdown here is the "I know how it sounded, but that's not what I meant!" moment.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Pragmatics revolution = language used to ACHIEVE something (Austin & Searle).
- Locutionary = the words; illocutionary = the intent/motive; perlocutionary = the effect on the listener.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

notes.title: Interactionism — Social Interactionist View (Bruner)
notes.body:
SOCIAL INTERACTIONIST VIEW — Jerome Bruner
- Language acquisition results from BOTH biological and environmental factors, but early SOCIAL INTERACTION is emphasized most.
- Language Acquisition Support System (LASS): infants interact with important others before they can talk, prompting caregivers to provide context-appropriate language; the social counterpart to Chomsky's LAD.
- Children are ACTIVE — they initiate communication and social interaction. As their skills grow, caregivers raise the complexity of their models (scaffolding).

CAREGIVER LANGUAGE
- Motherese / parentese (same thing): simple sentences, more repetition, repeating the child's words as models, longer pauses, exaggerated pitch variation. This eases imitation, increases exposure, highlights importance, and marks sentence boundaries.
- Expansion: the adult repeats what the child said but adds words, reorders, or adds structure to model greater complexity.
- Trevarthen: turn-taking develops through games and non-verbal exchange before words appear.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Social interactionist theorist = Bruner; key term = LASS (social counterpart to LAD).
- Motherese/parentese features and the role of EXPANSION.
- Children are initiators; scaffolding increases with ability.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

notes.title: Interactionism — Cognitive View (Piaget)
notes.body:
COGNITIVE VIEW — Jean Piaget
- Looks at the connection between cognitive development and language development.
- Language is NOT purely learned and NOT purely innate — we're born with cognitive PRECURSORS, and language emerges as a product of cognitive organization and development.
- Language develops as a means to process, organize, and understand the environment; repeated exposure strengthens some information-processing connections while others weaken.

SUPPORTING PHENOMENA (from the handout)
- Object permanence: by ~18 months children realize objects exist when out of sight; linked to the surge in object-label vocabulary.
- Seriation: a child must be able to order objects by size before learning comparatives like "bigger"/"smaller."

LIMITATIONS
- Clear links between language and intellect are traceable in the first ~18 months but become harder to find later.
- Syntax in particular doesn't seem to depend on general intellectual growth (some children speak fluently despite atypical cognitive development).

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Cognitive view: language follows/parallels cognitive development (Piaget).
- Object permanence (~18 mo) → vocabulary jump; seriation → comparatives.
- Limitation: syntax doesn't track general intelligence.
notes.source: Theories of Language Acquisition (handout)

notes.title: Interactionism — Semantic View (Fillmore)
notes.body:
OVERVIEW
Interactionist theories combine genetics AND environment (nature + nurture). Children are born prewired to notice structural clues and, paired with environmental exposure, learn their native language. Views within interactionism: semantic, cognitive, social interactionist, and the pragmatics revolution.

SEMANTIC VIEW — Charles Fillmore (generative semantic theory)
- Meaning comes not only from structure/grammar but from the RELATIONSHIPS between the words chosen.
- Adds a deeper level to Chomsky's LAD: universal concepts for how nouns and verbs relate (semantic, not just structural). Fillmore saw these as arising from genetic/environmental phenomena rather than simply prewired.
- Two parts of a sentence:
  • Modality — verb tense, negation, interrogation.
  • Proposition — the noun–verb relationship (most important to the semantic theory).
- Case: "a specific semantic role or function that can be filled by a particular type of noun phrase." The VERB determines which case its nouns take, and each case conveys different meaning.
- The seven cases (familiarize, don't memorize): agentive, dative, experiencer, factitive, instrumental, locative, objective.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Semantic view = MEANING via word relationships; theorist = Fillmore.
- Modality (tense/negation/question) vs. Proposition (noun–verb relationship = the core).
- Verbs determine the CASE of their nouns.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

notes.title: Nativism — Evidence & Limitations
notes.body:
CORE CLAIM (NATURE) — review
Chomsky: children are born prewired with a Language Acquisition Device (LAD) holding universal structural rules; impoverished, incomplete input can't explain how quickly and uniformly children acquire language. Transformational generative grammar: deep structure (meaning) → transformations → surface structure (spoken form).

EVIDENCE FOR INNATENESS
- Virtuous errors ("intelligent mistakes"): forms like "drinked" show children apply RULES, not mere imitation.
- Same developmental milestones across children and cultures, largely regardless of upbringing.
- Children often can't repeat a structure they haven't yet acquired (McNeill's "Nobody don't like me" exchange).
- Little explicit grammatical correction from parents (who care more about truth/politeness) — yet grammar still develops.
- Critical period: children who don't acquire language by ~age 7 never fully catch up — the case of Genie (isolated, discovered at 13; gained vocabulary but not full grammar).
- Human anatomy and dedicated brain areas (Broca's, Wernicke's); apes learn "words" but little/no grammar (Slobin/Pinker).
- Creoles: children turn a pidgin into a full, rule-governed language (Bickerton) — the LAD at work. Sign languages are full grammatical languages; deaf children pass through the same stages (a signing creole emerged in Nicaragua).
- Slobin's modification: the LAD may be a process mechanism for working out rules rather than a store of fixed categories.

LIMITATIONS OF CHOMSKY'S THEORY
- It is theoretical/grammar-focused; Chomsky didn't study real children or the interaction between children and caregivers, nor the FUNCTIONS/reasons a child wants to speak.
- The case of Jim (hearing son of deaf parents): TV/radio exposure wasn't enough; progress came only with interaction.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Virtuous errors + universal milestones + critical period (Genie) + creoles = the innateness argument.
- Critical period ≈ age 7; Genie is the classic case.
- Key limitation: ignores interaction and the functions of language.
notes.source: Theories of Language Acquisition (handout)

notes.title: Behaviorism — Deep Dive (Skinner)
notes.body:
CORE CLAIM (NURTURE)
Language is learned as something humans do to control or influence others, acquired through experience and exposure — "by imitation, reinforcement, and successive approximations toward adult language." Primary theorist: B.F. Skinner. (Skinner-based/ABA approaches often underlie intervention for children with autism and other developmental disabilities.)

OPERANT CONDITIONING
An operant is any behavior whose frequency is affected by the responses that follow it.
- Reinforcement INCREASES a behavior; punishment DECREASES a behavior.
- "Negative" ≠ bad — it means something is REMOVED from the environment.
- Four quadrants:
  • Positive reinforcement: add something good → behavior ↑
  • Negative reinforcement: remove something bad → behavior ↑
  • Positive punishment: add something bad → behavior ↓
  • Negative punishment: remove something good → behavior ↓

KEY MECHANISMS
- Discriminative stimulus: a prompt/cue before the target behavior (e.g., pointing to the letter L to cue /l/).
- Shaping: reinforcing successive approximations toward the target.
- Chaining: teaching the sequence of steps that make up a behavior.

FIVE VERBAL OPERANTS (Skinner)
1. Echoic — imitation of a present model.
2. Tact — labeling a thing or action.
3. Mand — requesting.
4. Intraverbal — social talk in situational context.
5. Autoclitic — combining words based on observation/experience.

CLASSICAL CONDITIONING (Pavlov)
A naturally occurring (unconditioned) response to an unconditioned stimulus is trained to occur in response to a neutral/conditioned stimulus. Applied to language: a baby comes to understand "sit" after repeated physical support to sit.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Behaviorism = NURTURE; Skinner = operant conditioning; Pavlov = classical conditioning.
- Reinforcement ↑, punishment ↓; positive = add, negative = remove.
- Memorize the 5 verbal operants: echoic, tact, mand, intraverbal, autoclitic.
- Discriminative stimulus (before), shaping (approximations), chaining (steps).
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture 3 (lecture notes)

notes.title: The Ear (Hearing Mechanism)
notes.body:
The ear has 3 parts: outer, middle, and inner.

OUTER EAR
- Pinna: the visible outer ear; directs sound into the ear canal.
- External auditory meatus: the ear canal.
- Tympanic membrane (eardrum): at the end of the ear canal; absorbs sound energy and vibrates.

MIDDLE EAR
- The eardrum is attached to a chain of tiny bones — the OSSICLES.
- Ossicles (3 bones): malleus (hammer) → incus (anvil) → stapes (stirrup).
- Sequence: eardrum vibrates the malleus → incus → stapes.
- The stapes is the 'footplate' and fits into the OVAL WINDOW, moving the fluids of the inner ear.

INNER EAR — two primary functions: hearing and balance
- Balance: the semicircular canals.
- Hearing: the cochlea (inside the temporal bone), spiral-shaped like a snail shell.
  - Nerve pathways spiral into a cone-shaped bone, the modiolus, which connects to the auditory nerve.
  - Sound/vibration enters the oval window → motion in the inner-ear fluids → movement of the tectorial membrane → triggers the inner hair cells (arranged by tone/frequency) → the auditory nerve carries messages to the brain.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- 3 parts: outer, middle, inner.
- Ossicles IN ORDER: malleus → incus → stapes.
- Stapes → oval window → inner-ear fluid motion.
- Cochlea = hearing; semicircular canals = balance.
- Full pathway: eardrum → ossicles → oval window → cochlear fluid → tectorial membrane → inner hair cells → auditory nerve → brain.
notes.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

notes.title: The Brain
notes.body:
The brain is divided into right and left hemispheres. Primary speech and language functions originate in the LEFT hemisphere.

KEY AREAS
- Wernicke's area: language comprehension and formulation.
- Arcuate fasciculus: transmits language information (connects Wernicke's area to Broca's area).
- Broca's area: motor planning and coordination of articulation.
- Motor cortex: sends signals to the speech mechanism to produce the speech that represents the formulated language.

NEURAL PATHWAY FOR SPEECH & LANGUAGE
- Central nervous system (CNS): the pathway along which messages travel from the brain to the muscles of speech.
  - Pyramidal system: controls refined, intricate movements (e.g., lips and tongue — the articulators).
  - Extrapyramidal system: controls more gross and unskilled motor movements.
- Peripheral nervous system (PNS): messages pass into the cranial and spinal nerves.
  - 12 pairs of CRANIAL nerves (transmit sensory and motor info); 6 are primarily associated with motor speech.
  - 31 pairs of SPINAL nerves; responsible for controlling respiration.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Left hemisphere dominance for speech/language.
- Wernicke's = comprehension; Broca's = articulation planning; arcuate fasciculus = the connection between them.
- Pyramidal = fine/refined; extrapyramidal = gross/unskilled.
- 12 pairs cranial nerves (6 for motor speech) · 31 pairs spinal nerves (respiration).
notes.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

notes.title: Resonation & Articulation
notes.body:
RESONATION
Resonation shapes the laryngeal tone by the size and shape of the pharynx, oral (mouth), and nasal cavities.
- Plays its most important role in shaping VOWEL sounds (open sounds with free airflow).
- We change sounds by changing the shape of the pharynx and mouth: opening wider or narrowing, moving the tongue, rounding the lips, etc.
- The velum (soft palate) can close the mouth off from the nasal cavity.

ARTICULATION
Sounds are refined further by articulation; it is hard to fully separate resonation from articulation.
- Most associated with shaping CONSONANT sounds.
- The ARTICULATORS: teeth, tongue, lips, alveolar ridge, hard palate, soft palate (velum), and jaw.
- Tongue moves rapidly to shape sounds.
- Soft palate (velum) moves up and back to close the mouth off from the nasal cavities.
- Alveolar ridge: the hard, bumpy ridge behind the top teeth.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Resonation → vowels; Articulation → consonants.
- Three resonating cavities: pharynx, oral, nasal.
- Be able to list all the articulators.
- Velum/soft palate role: opens/closes the passage to the nasal cavity.
notes.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

notes.title: Phonation
notes.body:
Phonation is the production of sound at the larynx ('voice box').
- Larynx PRIMARY function: protect the trachea and lungs from foreign material.
- Larynx SECONDARY function: sound production.

KEY CARTILAGES & STRUCTURES
- Thyroid cartilage: outer cartilage; may protrude as the 'Adam's apple'; vocal folds attach here.
- Cricoid cartilage: ring-shaped; sits within the thyroid at its base.
- Epiglottis: attached to the cricoid; minor role in speech but protects the windpipe during swallowing.
- Arytenoid cartilages: pyramid-shaped; sit atop the cricoid; have a vocal process and lateral process; muscles move them to open/close the vocal folds.
- Vocal folds: muscle + ligament; attach to the thyroid and the arytenoids.
- Glottis: the space between the vocal folds.
- Hyoid bone: supports the laryngeal region.
- Intrinsic muscles: ADDUCTORS bring the folds together (close the glottis); ABDUCTORS move them apart (open the glottis).

THE 5-STEP PHONATION PROCESS
1. Adduction of the vocal folds (folds brought together, airflow restricted).
2. Exhaled air pressure builds beneath the adducted folds.
3. Pressure blows the folds apart, releasing a puff of air into the trachea.
4. After the release, sub-fold pressure drops.
5. The pressure drop + fold elasticity snaps the folds back together — the cycle repeats.

Vibration rate: ~120–145 times/second in males; ~200–260 times/second in females.
The result is a glottal/laryngeal tone until it is shaped by resonation.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Larynx: protection FIRST, sound production SECOND.
- Know the 4 key cartilages: thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis, arytenoids.
- Glottis = space between the vocal folds.
- Adductors = together; abductors = apart. (See heads-up note — the lecture handout stated these reversed.)
- Be able to list the 5 steps of phonation and the male/female vibration rates.
notes.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

notes.title: Respiration
notes.body:
Breathing is both a life function and the first process of speech.
- Breathing for LIFE ≈ 50% inhalation / 50% exhalation.
- Breathing for SPEECH ≈ 15% inhalation / 85% exhalation (controlled exhalation extended up to ~15 seconds for speaking).

KEY ANATOMY
- Thoracic (thorax) cavity: contains the lungs, diaphragm, and 12 thoracic vertebrae; caged in by 12 pairs of ribs.
- Diaphragm: primary muscle of inhalation; sits just under the lungs; dome-shaped at rest.
- Abdomen: located below the diaphragm.
- Lungs: PASSIVE — they receive air; they do not actively suck air in.
- Trachea: the windpipe air travels through.

PHYSIOLOGY — BOYLE'S LAW
"If gas is kept at a constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional to one another and have a constant product."
- Inhalation: diaphragm contracts and flattens; ribs lift and swing up and out → thorax volume INCREASES → pressure DECREASES → air is forced into the lungs to equalize pressure.
- Exhalation: muscles of inhalation relax; diaphragm returns to its dome, ribs lower → thorax volume DECREASES → pressure INCREASES → air flows out of the lungs.
- One inhalation + one exhalation = one full cycle of respiration.

Respiration then feeds into phonation: the exhaled air is forced through points of constriction.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Life 50/50 vs. speech 15/85 breathing ratios.
- Diaphragm = primary muscle of inhalation; flattens on contraction.
- Lungs are passive; airflow is driven by pressure/volume (Boyle's Law), not by the lungs "pulling."
- Volume ↑ = pressure ↓ (air in); volume ↓ = pressure ↑ (air out).
notes.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

notes.title: Overview: Speech, Language & the Four Processes
notes.body:
Lecture 1 covers the four subsystems of speech, the brain, and the hearing mechanism.

SPEECH vs. LANGUAGE
- Language is largely innate; speech is learned (innate & learned).
- Key theme: "All of the structures involved in producing speech are designed for other, more basic biological purposes."

THE FOUR PROCESSES OF SPEECH (in order)
1. Respiration
2. Phonation
3. Resonation
4. Articulation

Each subsystem has a BIOLOGICAL function and a SPEECH function:
- Respiration — bio: breathing / O2–CO2 exchange · speech: provides the 'power' (airstream)
- Phonation — bio: airway protection · speech: produces sound
- Resonation — bio: filter/humidify air, eating · speech: shapes the sound from the vocal folds
- Articulation — bio: eating, moving the bolus · speech: restricts the airstream to form speech sounds

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Memorize the four processes IN ORDER: Respiration → Phonation → Resonation → Articulation.
- Be able to give both the bio and speech function for each subsystem.
- Speech structures are all "borrowed" from more basic biological systems.
notes.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

notes.title: Communication Foundations & Terminology
notes.body:
KEY TERMS (Connection of Brains)
- Communication: sending and receiving of information.
- Language: arbitrary symbols organized by rules characteristic of our culture.
- Receptive language: comprehension — listening (spoken) and reading (written).
- Expressive language: production — speaking, writing, and other forms (sign language, AAC devices).
- Speech: oral expression of language; articulation and shaping of sounds.
- Pragmatics: use of language for social interaction; the unwritten rules of relationships.
- Semantics: use of words to convey meaning; vocabulary.
- Syntax: grammar and rules for sentence structure.
- Morpheme: smallest unit of meaning.
- Suprasegmental: pitch, rate, stress — features that give character and meaning to speech.
- Echolalia: imitation of words/phrases without understanding meaning.

COMMUNICATION FRAMEWORK
- SPEECH components: Articulation, Phonology, Fluency, Voice.
- LANGUAGE components: Semantics, Morphology, Syntax, Pragmatics.
- Speech and language components influence one another (e.g., articulation/phonology errors can affect morphology; voice/intonation can change pragmatic meaning).

CHARACTERISTICS OF LANGUAGE
- Innate in humans.
- We learn the language we are exposed to.
- Exists in the mind.
- A system of arbitrary symbols.
- Rule-governed structure defined by our culture.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Receptive = comprehension (listen/read); Expressive = production (speak/write/sign/AAC).
- Know the SPEECH vs LANGUAGE split of the communication framework.
- Morpheme = smallest unit of MEANING (not sound).
- Echolalia = imitation WITHOUT understanding.
notes.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

notes.title: Hockett's Characteristics of Human Communication
notes.body:
Charles Hockett identified design features that help distinguish human communication from that of other species.

- Discreteness: messages are built from separate, distinct units.
- Interchangeability: a user can both send and receive the same messages.
- Semanticity & indexicality: signals carry stable meaning and can point to specific referents.
- Productivity: an infinite number of novel messages can be created.
- Displacement: we can talk about things removed in time and space (past/future/elsewhere).
- Duality of patterning: meaningless units (sounds) combine into meaningful units (words).
- Recursion: structures can be embedded within structures.
- Prevarication: language can be used to lie or deceive.
- Reflexivity: language can be used to talk about language itself.
- Learnability: a speaker of one language can learn another.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Be able to give a one-line example of each feature.
- Displacement and productivity are classic "what makes human language special" answers.
- Duality of patterning = sound level + meaning level.
notes.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

notes.title: The Speech Chain
notes.body:
The speech chain describes the connection between a speaker and a listener — a six-step process, "brain to brain."

SIX STEPS
1. Think ("internal"): the speaker forms and prepares the thought to be expressed.
2. The speaker selects the right words and grammatical forms and orders them correctly.
3. The speaker's brain sends messages to the speech muscles and systems.
4. The speech systems constrict airflow to produce vibrations in the larynx, creating air-pressure changes (sound waves / voice).
5. The sound waves reach the listener and are picked up by the hearing mechanism.
6. The listener's brain analyzes and interprets the neural impulses, recognizing the message.

FIVE LEVELS (as it crosses from speaker to listener)
Linguistic → Physiological → Acoustic → Physiological → Linguistic.
- Message originates in the brain (linguistic), brain-to-body forms speech (physiological), sound is produced (acoustic), the listener captures it (physiological), and the brain interprets it (linguistic).

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Memorize the level sequence: linguistic → physiological → acoustic → physiological → linguistic.
- "Brain to brain completes the speech chain."
- It all happens nearly instantly.
notes.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

notes.title: The Brain in Language (Review + New Concepts)
notes.body:
REVIEW — cortical language areas (from Module 1):
- Wernicke's area: finding the words we need and understanding language (comprehension).
- Arcuate fasciculus: connects and transports information from Wernicke's area to Broca's area.
- Broca's area: organizes and sends signals for how to physically produce speech.

NEW CONCEPTS this module:
- Mirror neurons: fire both when we perform an action AND when we observe others; theorized to support imitation and speech/language development. (In humans, the analog of monkey area F5 is Broca's area.)
- Mirror neuron system (MNS): the broader network; differences in the MNS have been linked to autism spectrum disorder.
- Plasticity: the brain's ability to change and adapt its structure and function with experience.
- Self-organizing neural network: the brain's storage/"filing system" for words (memory and organization); explains phenomena like the naming deficit and the age-of-acquisition effect.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Wernicke's = comprehension; Broca's = production; arcuate fasciculus = the connection.
- Mirror neurons: DOING and OBSERVING both trigger them.
- Plasticity = change with experience; supports the "language is innate" argument alongside dedicated brain structures.
notes.source: Connection of Brains (S. Herrera) — Module 2 deck

notes.title: Nature vs. Nurture & the Three Theory Families
notes.body:
The theories of language acquisition sit along a nature–nurture continuum.

- NATURE: development is driven by genetics/biology — "born this way."
- NURTURE: development is driven by environment and experience.

THREE FAMILIES
1. Nativism — argument for NATURE. Language is innate and biologically based; humans are pre-wired to acquire language (Chomsky, LAD, linguistic universals). Support: dedicated brain structures (Broca's, Wernicke's, arcuate fasciculus), mirror neurons, and plasticity.
2. Behaviorism — argument for NURTURE. Language is a learned behavior; the environment is the critical factor (Skinner, operant conditioning, reinforcement/punishment, "empty vessel").
3. Interactionism — a MODERATE view. Both biological and environmental factors matter; language develops in the social context of the child's interactions with caregivers.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Map each theory to nature / nurture / both.
- Nativism = nature; Behaviorism = nurture; Interactionism = both.
- Neither extreme fully discounts the other — the modern consensus is "both born and made."
notes.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

notes.title: Nativism — Deep Dive
notes.body:
CORE CLAIM
Language is innate, universal, and unique to humans. Nativists (biological nativists) argue oral language is instinctive and genetically coded, acquired with minimal environmental involvement; the environment merely triggers a natural biological process.

KEY IDEAS
- Noam Chomsky: figurehead; "all humans acquire language."
- Language Acquisition Device (LAD): innate reservoir of universal language-structure rules; takes the child's language input and generates the grammar of the native language.
- Linguistic universals: rules and structural relationships common to all languages — offered as evidence that language is part of being human.
- Competence vs. performance: nativists stress competence (underlying knowledge) over performance (actual use).
- Transformational generative grammar (Chomsky, 1957): language processed at two levels.
  - Phrase structure rules → DEEP structure: underlying relationships; universal across languages.
  - Transformations → SURFACE structure: rearrangement rules; language-specific.

BIOLOGY SUPPORT
- Specialized brain areas (Wernicke's, Broca's, arcuate fasciculus, motor cortex), mirror neurons, and plasticity.
- Genetic evidence: family-aggregation and twin studies; an autosomal-dominant pattern in some grammatical impairments; the SPCH1 region on chromosome 7q31 linked to speech/language deficits.

ANIMAL LANGUAGE STUDIES (limits of non-human "language")
- Washoe (chimp, Gardners): 100+ ASL signs, combined them, but no consistent grammar.
- Kanzi (bonobo, Savage-Rumbaugh): acquired symbols by exposure; showed some word-order comprehension.
- Overall: apes can acquire and combine symbols but show no adult-like syntax; supports the view that true language is uniquely human.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- LAD = innate, universal rules; deep structure = universal, surface structure = language-specific.
- Linguistic universals + rapid/early/universal acquisition = the nativist argument.
- Washoe = ASL/no grammar; Kanzi = learned by exposure/some word order.
notes.source: Born to Talk, Ch. 2: Language Acquisition — A Theoretical Journey

notes.title: Behaviorism
notes.body:
CORE CLAIM
Language is a learned behavior and the environment is the most critical factor (an argument for NURTURE).

KEY IDEAS
- B.F. Skinner: language acquired through operant conditioning.
- Operant conditioning: behavior shaped by consequences.
  - Reinforcement increases a behavior.
  - Punishment decreases a behavior.
- Empty vessel analogy: the child's mind is a blank container the environment fills.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Behaviorism = nurture; Skinner = operant conditioning.
- Reinforcement ↑ behavior; punishment ↓ behavior.
- A common nativist critique: children are exposed to complex, inconsistent input and rarely get explicit correction, yet still acquire language — hard to explain by reinforcement alone.
notes.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

notes.title: Interactionism & Its Views
notes.body:
CORE CLAIM
A moderate view on the nature–nurture continuum: both biological and environmental factors are important, and language develops in the social context of the child's interactions. The child's attempts to communicate prompt caregivers to model language. Key figures: Lev Vygotsky (Zone of Proximal Development) and Jean Piaget (language mirrors cognitive development).

THREE INTERACTIONIST VIEWS
1. Semantic view — shifts emphasis from structure to MEANING.
   - Fillmore's case grammar: structure dictated by the semantic relationship of verb & nouns.
   - Lois Bloom: context matters — both linguistic and non-linguistic information.
2. Cognitive view — language is NOT innate and NOT (purely) learned; it parallels cognitive development.
   - Piaget's sensorimotor period (birth–2): symbolic play parallels understanding that words = people, places, things.
   - Information Processing Theory.
3. Social interactionist view — biological and environmental factors both matter, but not equally.
   - Children interact socially before producing language; language develops from these interactions.
   - Focus on language USE (pragmatics); supported by parentese (child-directed speech).
   - Speech Act Theory: locutionary (the utterance), illocutionary (intended function), perlocutionary (effect on the listener).

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Vygotsky → ZPD; Piaget → sensorimotor / cognition-first.
- Semantic view → meaning (Fillmore/Bloom); Cognitive view → cognition (Piaget/IPT); Social view → USE/pragmatics (parentese, speech acts).
- Speech acts: locutionary = words, illocutionary = intent, perlocutionary = effect.
notes.source: Theories of Acquisition (B. Reece) — Module 2 deck

notes.title: Piaget's Cognitive Organization: Schema, Assimilation, Accommodation, Equilibrium
notes.body:
Jean Piaget studied how living things learn and how we organize cognitive information.

- Schema: our mental 'file-folder' system. We use our schemata to process, identify, store, and retrieve information; folders are arranged by relationships and commonalities.
- Assimilation: adding new information into an EXISTING schema.
- Accommodation: adding a NEW schema (or reorganizing) when information doesn't fit an existing folder.
- Equilibrium: keeping assimilation and accommodation in BALANCE. We tend to assimilate new info into a folder until enough accumulates to require reorganizing into a new schema.

PANTRY ANALOGY
Canned food vs. dry goods = two schemata. Chips → assimilate into 'dry goods.' Enough crackers/granola/cookies → accommodate by creating a 'snacks' area. The ongoing rebalancing = equilibrium.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Assimilation = fit into existing; Accommodation = make new/reorganize; Equilibrium = balance of the two.
- Schema = the file-folder system itself.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

notes.title: Piaget's Four Stages of Intellectual Development
notes.body:
Development is not just moving from one stage to the next — skills carry forward and are often PREREQUISITES for later stages.

1. Sensorimotor intelligence (birth-2): knowledge through senses + motor action; prerequisite to language; 6 substages.
2. Preoperational thought (2-7): rapid language growth; learning via hands-on visual/motor tasks; egocentric (hard to take others' perspectives); problem solving focuses on one element.
3. Concrete operations (7-11): logical thinking; reading/writing grow; still limited in ABSTRACT thinking.
4. Formal operations (11-15): abstract thinking; combines prior knowledge with new info; plans for tasks.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Memorize the four stages IN ORDER with ages: SM (0-2), Pre (2-7), Concrete (7-11), Formal (11-15).
- Abstract thinking = formal operations.
- Skills are carried forward and act as prerequisites.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

notes.title: Sensorimotor: The Six Key Skills
notes.body:
These six skills develop across the sensorimotor stage and are crucial for language and more complex thinking. (Perception underlies them: how we select, organize, integrate, and interpret input from the five senses; distancing lets us perceive from greater distances, leading toward naming and representation.)

1. Object permanence: things still exist even when outside the five senses (building a cognitive representation).
2. Causality: cause and effect — actions/events lead to other events.
3. Means/ends: using cause-and-effect to find the actions (means) that reach a goal (end), via actions or words.
4. Imitation: copying models seen/heard/felt (mirror neurons); progresses to delayed/deferred imitation.
5. Play: child-directed exploration; SYMBOLIC play (one object represents another) is crucial because words are symbolic representations.
6. Communication: conceptual development that feeds the child's growing language ability.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Know all six skills; object permanence and symbolic play are high-yield.
- Symbolic play ↔ language: words are symbols for things.
- Imitation → deferred imitation (from memory) is a later achievement.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)

notes.title: Sensorimotor: The Six Substages (birth-24 months)
notes.body:
Watch the six key skills change across the substages. (This is the framework used to rate a child's level per domain — e.g., play, communication, means-end.)

1. Substage 1 (birth-1 mo): world revolves around the infant; NO means-end or object concept; highly reflexive, automatic actions.
2. Substage 2 (1-4 mo): waking up to the world; vision improves, tracks/locates sounds; still no object separateness; pre-imitative behavior begins; communication via reflexive cries (discomfort, calling, requesting) and pleasure vocalizations; cooing/laughing by end.
3. Substage 3 (4-8 mo): moves/explores but stuck on the here-and-now; means/ends by coincidence (repeats actions for a result); imitation of previously-mastered behaviors; play = repeating actions with toys for pleasure; babbling (CV sounds) emerges. ('Mama'/'dada' aren't words until consistent, intentional, meaningful.)
4. Substage 4 (8-12 mo): object permanence BEGINS (searches for hidden objects); causality with intent; imitates unfamiliar and unseen behaviors; babbling may become first words / vocalizations + gestures.
5. Substage 5 (12-18 mo): object permanence only when the hiding is visible; causality uses people/tools as agents; experiments to problem-solve; communication = simple, intentional words.
6. Substage 6 (18-24 mo): REPRESENTATIONAL thinking (solve problems mentally by planning); object permanence FULLY developed; DEFERRED imitation (from memory); more complex pretend/auto-symbolic play.

NOTE: Later research shows babies move through these substages and show some skills EARLIER than Piaget thought, and knowledge includes perceptual (seen/heard) experiences, not only felt ones.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Object permanence: begins substage 4, fully developed substage 6.
- Deferred imitation + representational thought = substage 6.
- Substage 1 = reflexive, no object/means-end concept.
notes.source: COMM DIS 1B Lecture: Cognitive Development (Ch. 3, pp. 62-88)
